sections.title: Fútbol
sections.summary: Not a sport here. A religion with a fixture list.

classes.title: ¿De qué cuadro sos?
classes.summary: The five big clubs, the Superclásico and the question you can't dodge

pages.title: The question
pages.body: Meet someone new in Buenos Aires and within ten minutes you'll hear: **¿De qué cuadro sos?** — *Which team are you?* A **cuadro** is a club. It's not small talk: your club is inherited from your dad, your grandpa, your barrio. People change jobs, partners, even countries. Changing clubs? Never. **Cambiar de cuadro** is basically treason.
pages.fun_fact: Plenty of babies are signed up as club members (**socios**) days after being born.

pages.title: Los cinco grandes
pages.body: Five clubs are called **los cinco grandes** — *the big five*: **Boca Juniors**, **River Plate**, **Independiente**, **Racing Club** and **San Lorenzo**. They have the most fans and, historically, the most titles. Everyone else is a *chico* (small club) — though say that to a fan of Vélez or Estudiantes and you'll get a long lecture.

pages.prompt: Match the club to its nickname
pages.explain: **Xeneize** means *Genoese*: Boca was founded in 1905 by Italian immigrants' kids in La Boca. River got **Millonario** for spending big on players in the 1930s.

pages.title: El Superclásico
pages.body: **Boca vs River** is the **Superclásico** — the biggest rivalry in the country. A **clásico** is any derby; this one gets the *super*. Boca plays at **La Bombonera** (*the chocolate box*) in La Boca. River plays at **El Monumental** in Núñez. Funny detail: River was also born in La Boca, in 1901, and moved north later. Neighbors first, enemies forever.
pages.fun_fact: In 2018 they met in the Copa Libertadores final, and the second leg ended up being played in Madrid. River won.

pages.title: Insults with pride
pages.body: Rivals give each other nasty nicknames, and fans end up wearing them proudly. River fans call Boca fans **bosteros** (from **bosta**, *manure* — the story goes it was a dig at the smell by the Riachuelo). Boca fans call River fans **gallinas** (*chickens*, as in cowards), a name that stuck after River blew the 1966 Libertadores final against Peñarol. San Lorenzo fans are **cuervos** (*crows*), after the priest who founded the club.

pages.statement: If a River fan calls you a "bostero", they think you support Boca.
pages.explain: Exactly. And if you *do* support Boca, the correct reply is a proud smile. Being **bostero** is a badge of honor for them.

pages.title: Avellaneda: two stadiums, one block
pages.body: Just south of the city, in **Avellaneda**, live **Racing** (light blue and white) and **Independiente** (red). Their stadiums are only a few hundred meters apart — you can see one from the other. That's the **clásico de Avellaneda**. Independiente fans are the **Diablos Rojos**, *Red Devils*. Imagine sharing a street with the one team you hate most.

pages.scenario: You're staying in La Boca and a friend lends you a red-and-white River shirt because it's cold. You're about to walk to the kiosk next to the Bombonera on match day.
pages.prompt: What do you do?
options: Wear it, it's just a shirt
Wear it, but say you're a tourist
pages.explain: Never wear the rival's colors in the wrong barrio, especially on match day. Best case: jokes and dirty looks. Worst case: you really don't want to find out.

pages.scenario: A taxi driver asks: "¿De qué cuadro sos?" You don't follow football at all.
pages.prompt: What's the smoothest answer?
options: Pick the rival of whatever sticker is on his dashboard
pages.explain: Turning the question back is gold: he'll happily talk for the whole ride. Saying football is boring is legal, but it's a conversation killer.

pages.prompt: Ask your new friend which team they support
pages.translation: Which team are you (a fan of)?
pages.explain: **Cuadro** is the everyday word for club. **Cuadra** is a city block — useful, but not here.

example.en: Which team do you support?

vocabulary.note: Boca, River, Independiente, Racing, San Lorenzo.

vocabulary.en: Boca fan (rivals' insult, worn with pride)

vocabulary.note: Don't say it to a River fan unless you're friends.

example.en: Shall we go to the match on Sunday?

classes.title: La hinchada
classes.summary: Chants, drums and the mysterious thing called aguante

pages.title: Hincha, not fan
pages.body: A fan is a **hincha**, and all the fans together are **la hinchada**. The story goes that the word comes from a man in Montevideo who inflated (**hinchar**) the balls and shouted so hard he became famous. Whatever the origin: a hincha doesn't *watch* a match. A hincha *plays* it from the stands.
pages.fun_fact: **Hinchar** also means to annoy. "No me hinchés" = "Stop bugging me."

pages.title: Cantitos and the bombo
pages.body: The stands never go quiet. The hinchada sings **cantitos** (*chants*) for ninety minutes, often to the tune of old rock or cumbia songs, with lyrics that mix love for the club and creative insults for the rival. Keeping the beat is the **bombo**, a big bass drum. Add **trapos** (*banners*) and paper rain, and you've got the show.

pages.statement: In an Argentine stadium, fans sit quietly and clap after good plays.
pages.explain: Sitting? Quietly? In the **popular** (standing terraces) people jump, sing and push for the whole match. Clapping politely is for tennis.

pages.title: El aguante
pages.body: **Aguante** comes from **aguantar**, *to endure*. For a hincha it means loyalty that survives everything: rain, losses, even relegation. "**¡Aguante Racing!**" = *Long live Racing!* You also hear it outside football: "**¡Aguante el asado!**" The team can be losing 3–0 and the hinchada still sings — that's aguante.

pages.prompt: Cheer for your team, rioplatense style
pages.translation: Long live Boca! / Come on Boca!
pages.explain: **¡Aguante…!** + anything you love. It works for clubs, bands and even foods.

pages.title: The dark side: barras bravas
pages.body: Every big club has a **barra brava** (or just **la barra**): the organized hardcore group that leads the chants and carries the drums. Many are also tangled up in violence and shady business — resale, parking, politics. After years of deaths, visiting fans were banned in 2013. Talk of bringing them back comes up again and again, but at most league games you'll still see only one hinchada.

pages.scenario: At the stadium, a guy from the barra walks past and tells your section to stand up and sing.
pages.prompt: What's the smart move?
options: Explain that you paid for your seat
Stand up and at least pretend to sing
pages.explain: You're a guest in their church. Stand, clap, hum along. Arguing with the barra is never a good plan.

pages.prompt: Match the word to the thing
pages.explain: **Trapo** literally means *rag*. For the barras, losing your trapo to a rival is the ultimate humiliation.

pages.statement: If your team gets relegated, a real hincha with aguante stops going to the stadium.
pages.explain: The opposite! When River went down in 2011, its fans filled stadiums in the second division. Aguante is exactly for the bad times.

example.en: Come on Independiente!

vocabulary.note: Often just "la barra".

example.en: Stop bugging me.

classes.title: 1978, 1986 and the Diez
classes.summary: The first two World Cups and a guy called Diego

pages.title: La Selección
pages.body: When Argentina plays, the whole country stops. The national team is **la Selección**, or **la Albiceleste** (*the white and sky-blue*). Club rivalries freeze for ninety minutes — a bostero and a gallina hug when Argentina scores. The team has won three World Cups: **1978**, **1986** and **2022**.

pages.title: 1978: a cup with a shadow
pages.body: Argentina hosted and won in **1978**, beating the Netherlands 3–1 after extra time at El Monumental, with two goals from **Mario Kempes**. But the country was under a military dictatorship that used the cup as propaganda while people were disappearing. Many Argentines still feel torn about it. Some results, like the 6–0 over Peru, remain the subject of suspicion that was never proven.

pages.statement: Everyone in Argentina celebrates the 1978 World Cup without mixed feelings.
pages.explain: The players are respected, but the dictatorship context makes 1978 a sore, debated topic. Tread gently.

pages.title: Diego
pages.body: **Diego Armando Maradona** grew up poor in Villa Fiorito and became the greatest idol the country has ever had. He wore the **10**, so he's **el Diez** — or simply **el Diego**. He captained Argentina to the **1986** title in Mexico. Some people even joke about the *Iglesia Maradoniana*, a fan "church" with its own Christmas on his birthday, October 30.

pages.title: Mexico 1986 vs England
pages.body: Quarter-final, June 22, 1986, four years after the Falklands/**Malvinas** war. Minute 51: Diego punches the ball into the net and the referee allows it. He later called it **la Mano de Dios** — *the Hand of God*. Four minutes later he dribbles past half the English team from his own half and scores **el Gol del Siglo**, *the Goal of the Century*. Argentina won 2–1.
pages.fun_fact: Radio commentator Víctor Hugo Morales screamed "¡Barrilete cósmico!" — *cosmic kite* — and it became legend.

pages.prompt: Put Argentina vs England, 1986, in order
items: Maradona dribbles past four players and the keeper
pages.explain: The Hand of God and the Goal of the Century were only four minutes apart. Gary Lineker scored England's goal near the end.

pages.scenario: An English friend at an asado says: "Maradona cheated, that's it." Everyone goes quiet.
pages.prompt: How do most Argentines see the Mano de Dios?
options: A shameful moment they'd rather forget
A cheeky bit of viveza, with a lot of history behind it
pages.explain: For many it's **viveza criolla** (street-smart cunning) and a symbolic revenge after Malvinas. Plenty of people also admit it was a handball. Expect a passionate debate, not agreement.

pages.prompt: What's the famous handball called?
pages.translation: The Hand of God
pages.explain: **Mano** is feminine even though it ends in -o: *la mano*.

pages.statement: Argentina won the 1986 final against West Germany.
pages.explain: 3–2 in the Azteca stadium. Jorge Burruchaga scored the winner after a pass from — who else — Diego.

vocabulary.en: the Hand of God (1986 handball goal)

example.en: We won the '86 World Cup.

vocabulary.note: Admired and criticized in equal measure.

classes.title: Messi and Qatar
classes.summary: Heartbreak in Brazil, glory in Qatar

pages.title: The quiet kid from Rosario
pages.body: **Lionel Messi** was born in **Rosario** in 1987 and left for Barcelona at 13. For years some Argentines grumbled that he didn't sing the anthem and only shone in Spain. He's a **Newell's** fan, by the way, and nicknamed **la Pulga** (*the flea*) for being small. That grumbling is now very, very dead.

pages.title: 2014: so close
pages.body: The **2014** final in Rio's Maracanã: Argentina vs Germany, 0–0 into extra time. In minute 113, **Mario Götze** scored. Germany 1–0. Messi was named best player of the tournament and looked at the trophy he couldn't touch. Then came two lost Copa América finals, in 2015 and 2016. After 2016, Messi briefly retired from the Selección.

pages.statement: Argentina lost the 2014 World Cup final to Brazil.
pages.explain: It was **Germany**, 1–0, played in Brazil. Losing in Brazil's own stadium, to anyone, stung extra.

pages.title: Qatar 2022
pages.body: December 18, 2022. The final against France was madness: Argentina 2–0, then Mbappé scores twice in two minutes, Messi makes it 3–2 in extra time, Mbappé again: 3–3. Penalties. **Dibu Martínez**, the **arquero** (*goalkeeper*), saves one, and **Gonzalo Montiel** scores the last. Messi finally lifts the cup. Argentina's third star.
pages.fun_fact: The celebration in Buenos Aires drew millions of people — the Obelisco disappeared under a sea of shirts.

pages.prompt: Put the Qatar 2022 final in order
pages.explain: 4–2 on penalties. Many Argentines say they didn't breathe for about three hours.

pages.title: Muchachos
pages.body: The soundtrack of Qatar was a cantito: **"Muchachos, ahora nos volvimos a ilusionar"** — *Guys, now we've got our hopes up again*. Fans wrote it to the tune of a song by the band La Mosca. It name-checks Malvinas, Diego and Leo. Sing it at any party and the whole room joins in.

pages.scenario: It's a Selección match day and your Argentine friend has worn the same unwashed socks for every game since the tournament started.
pages.prompt: What's going on?
options: It's a cábala — a lucky ritual
pages.explain: A **cábala** is a superstitious ritual. Same seat, same socks, same mate. If the team wins, you do NOT change anything.

pages.prompt: Match the hero to the moment
pages.explain: Four finals, four names every Argentine knows — including the German one, sadly.

pages.prompt: Your friend is scared to change his lucky socks. He says:
pages.translation: I'm not washing them, it's a lucky ritual.
pages.explain: **Mufa** is bad luck (or the person who brings it) — the exact opposite.

example.es: El Dibu es el mejor arquero.
example.en: Dibu is the best goalkeeper.

vocabulary.note: Plural: penales. "Ir a penales" = go to a shootout.

example.en: Don't watch, you're a jinx.

vocabulary.note: La final = the final match. El final = the ending.

classes.title: Talk like a hincha
classes.summary: Golazos, gambetas, caños and the Sunday picado

pages.title: Potrero and picado
pages.body: Argentines say their football was born in the **potrero** — a dirt lot where kids play with a ball, a couple of stones as goalposts and zero rules. A casual game with friends is a **picado**. "¿Armamos un picado?" = *Shall we get a game together?* Today it's usually **fútbol 5** on synthetic grass, then beers.
pages.fun_fact: Calling a player "**de potrero**" is a big compliment: street-smart, creative, fearless.

pages.title: Gambeta and caño
pages.body: A **gambeta** is a dribble, the twisty, dancing kind Maradona and Messi made famous. A **caño** is a nutmeg: the ball between the defender's legs. Getting a caño in a picado means your friends will remind you for weeks. And a **golazo** is a stunning goal. The **-azo** ending makes anything bigger: **golazo**, **partidazo**.

pages.prompt: Match the word to its meaning

pages.scenario: In a picado, you slip the ball between the legs of your friend Nacho and run past him. Everyone screams.
pages.prompt: What did you just do?
pages.explain: **¡Caño!** Nacho will now be teased until the next picado. Maybe longer.

pages.title: El DT and the arquero
pages.body: The coach is **el DT** (*de-té*), short for **director técnico**. Every Argentine is secretly a DT: they all know who should play. The goalkeeper is **el arquero** (from **arco**, *goal*). And the defender who kicks everything in sight, ball or ankles? A **hachero**, an *axe man*.

pages.statement: In Argentina, "el DT" is the team's doctor.
pages.explain: **DT** = **director técnico**, the coach. Lionel Scaloni, the DT who won Qatar, gave his name to the team's nickname: **la Scaloneta**.

pages.title: Hacer la previa
pages.body: Before any big match you **hacer la previa**: meet up earlier to eat, drink, sing and get in the mood. The previa can last longer than the match itself. After the game, win or lose, there's analysis at the bar until late. Watching football alone? Suspicious behavior.

pages.prompt: Invite your friends to meet up before the Superclásico
pages.translation: Shall we do the pre-match hangout at my place?
pages.explain: Careful: a **picada** is a snack board of cheese and salami — very welcome at the previa, but not the same word.

pages.prompt: A perfect Superclásico Sunday, in order
items: Analyze every play at the bar

pages.scenario: Your team lost 4–0. Your Argentine friend's phone keeps buzzing with memes from rival fans.
pages.prompt: What's the local tradition here?
options: Mute everyone and disappear until Monday
Take the gastada, then return it when your team wins
pages.explain: A **gastada** is the teasing after a loss. You take it, you keep a list, and you pay it back with interest.

example.en: Shall we get a game together?

vocabulary.en: dirt lot where kids play football
to hang out before an event

example.es: Hacemos la previa en lo de Juan.
example.en: We're meeting at Juan's place first.

classes.title: Beyond Buenos Aires
classes.summary: Rosario, Córdoba, La Plata, and the women who got there first

pages.title: Not everything is Boca-River
pages.body: Porteños forget it, but some of the fiercest rivalries are outside the capital. Argentines call the rest of the country **el interior**, and in cities like **Rosario**, **Córdoba** and **La Plata** the local **clásico** matters far more than the Superclásico. Ask a rosarino about Boca and River and you'll get a shrug. Ask about Newell's and Central and cancel your plans.

pages.title: Rosario: leprosos vs canallas
pages.body: **Rosario Central** (1889) against **Newell's Old Boys** (1903, named after the English teacher Isaac Newell, whose former students founded it). The story goes that both were invited to a charity match for a leprosy clinic. Newell's said yes and became the **leprosos** (lepers); Central said no and became the **canallas** (scoundrels). Both now wear the insults with pride.

pages.statement: Messi and Di María are both from Rosario and support the same club.
pages.explain: Same city, opposite sides: Messi played in **Newell's** youth teams, Di María came up at **Central** and went back to play there. Rosario family dinners have survived worse.

pages.title: Córdoba and La Plata
pages.body: In Córdoba it's **Belgrano**, the **Piratas**, against **Talleres**, **la T** or the **Matadores**. They've met hundreds of times, and Belgrano fans still celebrate 2011, when they sent River down to the B. In La Plata, **Estudiantes** fans are **pinchas** (from *pincharratas*, 'rat-stabbers') and **Gimnasia**, founded in 1887, are the **triperos** or **el Lobo**.

pages.prompt: Match the club to its fans' nickname

pages.scenario: Your first night in Rosario. A new friend pours you a beer and asks: "¿Sos leproso o canalla?"
pages.prompt: What are they asking?
options: Are you from Rosario or Buenos Aires?
pages.explain: It's the Rosario version of **¿de qué cuadro sos?** If you don't have a team, say so with a smile. Picking one at random can cost you friends.

pages.title: The pioneers
pages.body: On **21 August 1971**, at an unofficial women's World Cup in Mexico, Argentina beat England **4–1** in the Estadio Azteca, in front of a huge crowd. **Elba Selva** scored all four. That's why 21 August is the **Día de la Futbolista**. It took until **2019**, after player Macarena Sánchez fought for real contracts, for the women's league to go semi-professional.

pages.statement: Argentina's women's team once beat England 4–1 at the Estadio Azteca.
pages.explain: 1971, all four goals by Elba Selva. Fifteen years before Diego's famous goals against England at the same stadium.

pages.prompt: Tell your friend what 21 August is
pages.text: Hoy es el Día de la ___.
pages.translation: Today is the Day of the (Woman) Footballer.
pages.explain: **Futbolista** works for men and women; **la futbolista** is a woman who plays.

vocabulary.en: the rest of the country (outside Buenos Aires)
vocabulary.note: Some people outside Buenos Aires find the term a bit porteño-centric.

example.es: Es futbolista y juega en Boca.

classes.title: The table, the drop and the VAR
classes.summary: Promedios, irse a la B and everything you'll hear on TV

pages.title: Fixture, fecha, tabla
pages.body: The season calendar is the **fixture** (say *fíxtur*), and each round is a **fecha**. After every fecha people check the **tabla** (league table): three points for a win, one for an **empate** (draw). A 5–0 is a **goleada** (thrashing). On Monday, the office talks about nothing else.

pages.title: The nightmare: el descenso
pages.body: The worst thing that can happen to a club is the **descenso** (relegation), or **irse a la B**, going down to the B. The dream of the smaller clubs is the **ascenso** (promotion). Even giants have fallen: San Lorenzo in 1981, Racing in 1983, River in 2011, Independiente in 2013. **Boca** never has, and Boca fans never let anyone forget it.

pages.statement: Among the cinco grandes, Boca Juniors is the only one that has never been relegated.
pages.explain: San Lorenzo, Racing, River and Independiente all went down at some point. It's Boca's favorite chant against every one of them.

pages.title: Promedios
pages.body: Here's a very Argentine twist: relegation isn't only about this season. Part of it depends on the **promedio**, your points per match averaged over the last three seasons. One great year can't save a struggling club, and one bad year rarely sinks a big one. Critics have long said that's exactly the point: to protect the big clubs. The rules change often; the promedios keep coming back.

pages.scenario: Your team is fifth this season, but your friend is still nervous about "los promedios".
pages.prompt: Why?
options: The last two seasons were terrible, and they still count
The VAR can take points away
pages.explain: Promedios drag the past along with you. A club that just came up is especially at risk: it has only a few matches to average, so every loss hurts.

pages.title: ¿Fue penal?
pages.body: Every tight call now goes to **el VAR** (say *el var*), and the debate lasts days: **¿fue penal?** (was it a penalty?), **¿estaba en offside?** Old-timers still say **orsai**, the way their grandparents pronounced offside. Some say the VAR killed the goal scream, since you wait before celebrating. Others say the ref was robbing us anyway, so at least now it's on camera.

pages.explain: **Irse a la B** = get relegated. Said with real fear, even when the second division isn't literally called 'B' anymore.

pages.statement: "Irse a la B" means your team got promoted.
pages.explain: It means going down. Going up is **subir** or **ascender**, and the promoted team's fans sing about it for years.

sections.title: Tango
sections.summary: The sad, sexy music of the Río de la Plata, and how not to embarrass yourself at a milonga

classes.title: Born on the edge of town
classes.summary: Two cities, one port, and a German squeezebox

pages.title: From the arrabal
pages.body: Tango was born in the late 1800s in the **arrabal**, the rough outskirts of the city: shared patios in **conventillos**, corner bars, the port. It was the music of immigrants, sailors, workers and **compadritos** (local tough guys with a knife and a nice hat). Polite society thought it was scandalous. Which, obviously, made it more popular.

pages.title: Buenos Aires AND Montevideo
pages.body: Careful here: tango isn't only porteño. It grew up on both sides of the **Río de la Plata**, in Buenos Aires and in **Montevideo**. Uruguayans will remind you, with love and zero patience. The most famous tango of all, **La Cumparsita**, was written by a Uruguayan, Gerardo Matos Rodríguez, and premiered in a Montevideo café in 1917.
pages.fun_fact: In 2009 Argentina and Uruguay went to UNESCO together, and tango became Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

pages.scenario: You're in Montevideo and you say: "I love Argentine tango!" Your Uruguayan friend raises an eyebrow.
pages.prompt: What's the safer thing to say?
pages.explain: **Rioplatense** means from the Río de la Plata, so it covers both cities. It's even how UNESCO put it. Your friend will lower the eyebrow.

pages.title: Men danced with men
pages.body: Around 1900 there were way more men than women in the city, because most immigrants were young single guys. So men often practiced tango **with each other**, on the street corner or in the patio, to the sound of an **organito** (a street barrel organ). Getting good mattered: you had to be decent before anyone would dance with you.

pages.statement: Tango started as elegant ballroom music for the rich in Buenos Aires.
pages.explain: The opposite. It was born among the poor and the rough, and the upper class only fully embraced it after it became a craze in **Paris**, around 1913. Nothing like European approval to change a porteño's mind.

pages.title: A squeezebox from Germany
pages.body: The sound of tango is the **bandoneón**, and it's German. The name comes from **Heinrich Band**, who sold them in the mid-1800s, supposedly so small churches with no organ could have music. Sailors and immigrants brought it to the Río de la Plata in the late 1800s; nobody's sure who brought the first one. From church hymns to brothel music in one boat trip.

pages.title: The fueye
pages.body: Tangueros call the bandoneón **el fueye**, from *fuelle* (bellows). It's famously hard: dozens of buttons, and each one plays a *different note* depending on whether you open or close it. Old German-made ones are still the most wanted, and a good one costs a small fortune.

pages.prompt: Where does the bandoneón come from?
pages.explain: Germany. And yes, the name comes from a person: Heinrich **Band**. The instrument of Argentine melancholy started in Lutheran Germany.

classes.title: Gardel
classes.summary: The voice, the smile, and the question of where he was born

pages.title: El Zorzal
pages.body: **Carlos Gardel** is *the* tango singer. Slicked-back hair, a smile that sold records, a voice people still call perfect. His nicknames: **el Zorzal criollo** (the local songbird) and **el Morocho del Abasto** (the dark-haired guy from Abasto, the market neighborhood where he grew up). His old house there is now a museum, and there's even a subway station named after him.

pages.title: Toulouse or Tacuarembó?
pages.body: Where was he born? Most researchers say **Toulouse, France**, in 1890, as Charles Romuald Gardes, son of a single mother who brought him to Buenos Aires as a toddler. But in 1920 Gardel himself signed papers saying he was born in **Tacuarembó, Uruguay**, in 1887. Many Uruguayans believe that version, and new documents keep reopening the fight: the latest, backing Tacuarembó, made headlines in January 2026.

pages.statement: Everyone in Argentina and Uruguay agrees on where Gardel was born.
pages.explain: Not even close. Toulouse has the French birth record; Tacuarembó has Gardel's own 1920 declaration. Argentines just say he's porteño, since that's where he grew up. Everyone claims him.

pages.title: Medellín, 1935
pages.body: On **June 24, 1935**, at the peak of his fame, Gardel died when his plane crashed on the runway in **Medellín**, Colombia, during a tour. He was 44. His lyricist **Alfredo Le Pera** died with him. The country went into mourning, and the myth started right there.

pages.title: Cada día canta mejor
pages.body: The classic line about Gardel: **cada día canta mejor**, "he sings better every day". Nobody knows who said it first, but it's the perfect joke: he's been dead since 1935 and he keeps improving. At his tomb in **Chacarita**, fans put a lit **pucho** (cigarette) between the fingers of his bronze statue. Legend says if it burns all the way, your wish comes true.

pages.scenario: Your friend's uncle, a Gardel fanatic, says: "Gardel murió en el 35, pero cada día canta mejor."
pages.prompt: What's he saying?
options: That the old recordings were remastered
That Gardel's legend keeps growing, even decades after he died
That a new singer sounds just like Gardel
pages.explain: It's affection and a joke at the same time. For tangueros, Gardel isn't a dead singer, he's a permanent presence.

pages.prompt: Your friend keeps complaining about something you can't fix. What do you tell them?
pages.translation: Ugh, go sing it to Gardel. (Go tell someone who cares.)
pages.explain: **Andá a cantarle a Gardel** is a cheeky way to brush someone off. Dicen que it started because of all the bad imitators singing at his tomb every June 24.

pages.title: Día Nacional del Tango
pages.body: Argentina celebrates the **Día Nacional del Tango** on **December 11**, since 1977. Why that day? It's Gardel's birthday, and also the birthday of **Julio De Caro**, a violinist and bandleader who changed how tango was played. Two birthdays, one party, lots of milongas.

classes.summary: The golden age of the orquestas, and the man they called tango's assassin

pages.title: The golden age
pages.body: In the **1940s**, tango was pop music. Every club, radio station and neighborhood dance had an **orquesta típica**: bandoneones, violins, piano and double bass, often with a singer. People followed bandleaders like football teams. Friday night meant going to hear *your* orquesta, and arguing about it on the way home.

pages.title: Four names to know
pages.body: **Juan D'Arienzo**, **el Rey del Compás** (the King of the Beat): punchy, rhythmic, made people dance. **Aníbal Troilo**, **Pichuco**, maybe the most loved bandoneón player ever. **Carlos Di Sarli**, **el Señor del Tango**: smooth and elegant. **Osvaldo Pugliese**: dark, dramatic, deep. Tango DJs still build whole nights around these four.

pages.prompt: Match the bandleader to his nickname or style

pages.title: A red carnation on the piano
pages.body: Pugliese was a member of the Communist Party and was jailed more than once for it, most famously in 1956. When he couldn't show up, his orquesta played anyway, with a **clavel rojo** (red carnation) on the empty piano. Everyone in the room got the message. At 80, in 1985, he packed the **Teatro Colón**, just where his mom always said he would end up.

pages.statement: When Pugliese was in prison, his orquesta cancelled all its shows.
pages.explain: They kept playing, with a red carnation on the piano instead of him. A silent protest everyone understood.

pages.title: Piazzolla breaks the rules
pages.body: **Astor Piazzolla**, from Mar del Plata, played bandoneón in Troilo's orquesta as a young man. In 1954 he went to Paris to study classical music with **Nadia Boulanger**, who told him to stop hiding tango and build on it. He came back and mixed tango with jazz and classical: **tango nuevo**. Think **Libertango** and **Adiós Nonino**.

pages.title: "That's not tango!"
pages.body: The traditionalists hated it. Piazzolla got called **el asesino del tango** (tango's assassin). Radios wouldn't play him, and "eso no es tango" followed him for years. He answered that it was *música contemporánea de Buenos Aires*. Today he's one of the most played Argentine composers in the world, and the old argument still starts fights at family dinners.

pages.scenario: At a dinner, the grandpa says Piazzolla ruined tango. The grandson says Piazzolla saved it.
pages.prompt: What are they reenacting?
options: The old debate between tango traditionalists and tango nuevo
pages.explain: The oldest **grieta** (divide) in tango: can you dance to it or is it concert music? Piazzolla wrote to be *listened* to, which is exactly what bugged the dancers.

items: Studies in Paris with Nadia Boulanger

classes.title: What tango sings about
classes.summary: Mom, the barrio, the woman who left, and a world gone wrong

pages.title: Three minutes of heartbreak
pages.body: Tango lyrics have favorite subjects. **La mina que se fue**, the woman who left (and it's always her fault). **La vieja**, mom, a saint. **El barrio**, the neighborhood as it used to be. And **nostalgia** for everything: youth, friends, the old café. Discépolo put it best: **el tango es un pensamiento triste que se baila**, a sad thought you can dance to.

pages.title: Lunfardo in the lyrics
pages.body: Early tango lyrics are full of **lunfardo**, the Buenos Aires street slang. **Mina** is a woman, still used today. **Percanta** is a woman too, but now you'll only hear it in old tangos. **Bulín** is a bachelor pad. **Garufa** is a night out partying. Some of these words survived only because tango kept singing them.

pages.prompt: Match the lunfardo word

pages.title: Mi Buenos Aires querido
pages.body: Gardel and his lyricist **Le Pera** wrote **Mi Buenos Aires querido** in 1934: a man far away, dreaming of seeing the city again. The famous line: **"cuando yo te vuelva a ver, no habrá más penas ni olvido"** (when I see you again, there'll be no more sorrow or forgetting). Every Argentine living abroad has cried to it at least once.

pages.title: Volver
pages.body: **Volver** (to return), also Gardel and Le Pera, is about coming back older to a city and a love you left. It has maybe the most quoted line in tango: **"que veinte años no es nada"** (twenty years is nothing). People say it at reunions, birthdays, anywhere time has passed and everyone pretends it hasn't.

pages.prompt: You run into an old school friend after ages. What do you say, quoting Volver?
pages.translation: Unbelievable! Twenty years is nothing.
pages.explain: Straight out of **Volver**. Every Argentine will get the reference, and probably start humming.

pages.title: Cambalache: the angry one
pages.body: **Cambalache** (1934), by **Enrique Santos Discépolo**, isn't about love. It says the 20th century is a mess where "lo mismo un burro que un gran profesor" (a donkey and a great professor, same thing): **"el mundo fue y será una porquería"** (the world was and will be garbage). In 1943 the military government banned it from the radio, and the ban lasted until 1949. It still sounds like this morning's news.
pages.fun_fact: A **cambalache** is a junk shop where everything is thrown together. People still say "¡esto es un cambalache!" about a total mess.

pages.statement: Cambalache was banned by Argentine governments.
pages.explain: Censored from 1943, when the military government went after lunfardo lyrics, until Perón lifted the ban in 1949. Being banned only made it more famous.

pages.scenario: A friend looks at the chaos at a government office and sighs: "Esto es un cambalache."
pages.prompt: What do they mean?
pages.explain: Thanks to Discépolo, **cambalache** means a mess where nothing makes sense and nobody plays fair. The tango turned a shop into a worldview.

classes.title: At the milonga
classes.summary: The unwritten rules of the dance floor, and tango today

pages.title: What's a milonga?

word.en: a dance night, and a rhythm

pages.body: A **milonga** is a tango dance night: a hall, tables around a wooden floor, music from a DJ or a live orquesta, and people of every age dancing until late. (It's also a faster, bouncier rhythm related to tango, so yes, you can dance a milonga at the milonga.) There are milongas every night of the week in Buenos Aires.

pages.title: The cabeceo
pages.body: Nobody walks up and asks "¿bailamos?" at a traditional milonga. You use the **mirada** (look) and the **cabeceo** (a small nod). You catch someone's eye from across the room and nod. If they nod back, you go get them. If they look away, no one got rejected in public. Genius.

pages.scenario: At a milonga, you catch someone's eye and nod. They look down at their shoes.
pages.prompt: What happened?
options: They didn't see you, walk over and ask
They said no, politely. Try someone else.
They want you to nod again, harder
pages.explain: Looking away is the polite **no**. Walking over anyway puts them on the spot, and that's exactly what the **cabeceo** exists to avoid.

pages.title: Tandas and cortinas
pages.body: The music comes in **tandas**: sets of 3 or 4 songs of the same style and usually the same orquesta. Between tandas, the DJ plays a **cortina** (curtain), a short bit of non-tango music. That's the signal: everyone leaves the floor and changes partners. Many milongas end the night with **La Cumparsita**.

pages.title: Gracias = I'm done
pages.body: Same trap as with mate. You dance the whole tanda with your partner. If you say **gracias** after the first song, it doesn't mean "thanks", it means "thanks, **that's enough**". Your partner will walk you back to your table. Want to keep going? Just smile and wait for the next song.

pages.statement: At a milonga, it's polite to say "gracias" after every song.
pages.explain: **Gracias** ends the tanda. Say it after one song and you just dumped your partner, politely but clearly.

pages.title: The ronda
pages.body: Couples move around the floor in a **ronda**, counterclockwise, like cars on a track. No passing, no stopping to chat, no big kicks that hit the couple behind you. And never **teach on the floor**: correcting your partner mid-dance is a big no. Save it for class, or better, for never.

pages.prompt: A night at the milonga, in order
items: Meet on the floor and join the ronda
Say gracias and go back to your tables

pages.title: Show or milonga?
pages.body: Tourists often see tango at a **cena show**: dinner, sequins, flying legs, a rose in someone's mouth. Porteños call it **tango for export**. It's real skill, but it's stage tango. At a milonga, the dance is small, close and improvised. Each August the city hosts the **Mundial de Tango**, held since 2003, with a stage category and a **pista** (social floor) one.

pages.scenario: You want to see how porteños actually dance tango, not a show.
pages.prompt: Where do you go?
options: A dinner show with a set menu
A neighborhood milonga, even just to watch
pages.explain: At a **milonga** you can sit, have a drink and watch. Nobody minds, as long as you stay off the floor until you know the **códigos**.

sections.title: Música

classes.title: Rock nacional
classes.summary: Rock in Spanish, born in a café bathroom and raised under a dictatorship

pages.title: Born in a bathroom
pages.body: In 1967, **Los Gatos** released **"La balsa"** (*The raft*). Legend says Litto Nebbia and Tanguito finished it in the bathroom of **La Perla del Once**, a 24-hour café, to dodge the waiters who kept kicking them out for being loud. It sold over 250,000 copies, proof that rock sung in Spanish could sell. **Rock nacional** was born.
pages.fun_fact: **Rock nacional** doesn't mean patriotic rock. It means rock made here, and sung in Spanish.

pages.statement: "Rock nacional" is Argentine rock sung mostly in Spanish, not a genre about patriotism.
pages.explain: Right. The big idea of the 60s was simple and radical: you can rock in *castellano*. Before that, rock meant singing in English or copying the Beatles.

pages.title: El Flaco and Charly
pages.body: Two names you must know. **Luis Alberto Spinetta**, **el Flaco** (*the skinny one*), wrote poetic songs with his band **Almendra**, like **"Muchacha (ojos de papel)"** (1970). **Charly García** started as a teenager in the duo **Sui Generis** with Nito Mestre. Their goodbye at the **Luna Park** in 1975, two shows for about 30,000 people, became a famous live album and film: **Adiós Sui Generis**.

pages.title: Singing in code
pages.body: During the 1976–83 dictatorship, rock was watched, censored and harassed. So musicians wrote in metaphors. Charly's band **Serú Girán** (1978) filled stadiums with songs that said things *without saying them*. Their show at **La Rural** in December 1980 drew about 60,000 people. For many kids, a rock concert was the only place they could feel free together.

pages.title: The Malvinas paradox
pages.body: In April 1982, with the Malvinas war, the military government pushed radios to stop playing music **en inglés**. The same regime that had harassed rockers suddenly needed Spanish songs to fill the airwaves. Rock nacional exploded. Many musicians used the moment to ask for peace: in May, the **Festival de la Solidaridad Latinoamericana** gathered thousands at Obras Sanitarias.

pages.scenario: It's May 1982. You turn on the radio in Buenos Aires.
pages.prompt: What are you most likely to hear?
options: The Beatles and Queen, as usual
Argentine rock and folklore in Spanish
pages.explain: English-language music was pulled off the air during the war, so local rock and folklore took over. Plenty of bands went from underground to mainstream almost overnight.

pages.title: Gracias totales
pages.body: In the 80s came **Soda Stereo**: Gustavo **Cerati**, Zeta Bosio and Charly Alberti. They took Argentine rock across all of Latin America. At their farewell at River's stadium in September 1997, Cerati closed with a line everyone still quotes: **"¡Gracias… totales!"**. Today people say it, half joking, to thank someone *big time*.
pages.fun_fact: Fito Páez's **El amor después del amor** (1992), with guests like Spinetta, Charly, Cerati and Mercedes Sosa, is the best-selling album in Argentine rock history.

pages.prompt: A friend lends you their car for the weekend. How do you thank them, Cerati style?
pages.translation: Thanks… totally!
pages.explain: **Gracias totales** is Cerati's goodbye from 1997. Say it and every Argentine gets the reference.

pages.prompt: Put these rock nacional moments in order
items: Sui Generis says goodbye at the Luna Park

Radios stop playing English songs during Malvinas
pages.explain: 1967, 1975, 1980, 1982, 1997. Thirty years from a café bathroom to a full River stadium.

pages.explain: March 3, 2000, Hotel Aconcagua, Mendoza. He survived. Charly stories like this are part of the legend, and people tell them with affection.

classes.title: Folklore, peñas and pañuelos
classes.summary: Guitars, handkerchiefs and the voice of La Negra

pages.title: Folklore is not old stuff
pages.body: In Argentina **folklore** is a living music scene, not a museum. It's the music of the provinces: guitars, the **bombo legüero** (a deep drum made of wood and hide), violins and voices. It has many rhythms, like **zamba**, **chacarera** and **chamamé**, and young people still sing it at parties, especially in the north.

pages.title: La Negra
pages.body: **Mercedes Sosa**, from Tucumán, was **La Negra**, a nickname of affection. In October 1978 she was arrested on stage mid-concert in La Plata, with her audience. She went into exile in Europe. In February 1982, still under the dictatorship, she came back for a run of packed shows at the **Teatro Ópera** in Buenos Aires. Her version of Violeta Parra's **"Gracias a la vida"** still makes whole rooms cry.

pages.statement: In Argentina, calling Mercedes Sosa "La Negra" is an insult.
pages.explain: It was her nickname, used with love. In Argentina **negro/negra** is a very common nickname for friends and family, though, like everywhere, tone and context matter a lot.

pages.title: The one who came from far away
pages.body: **Atahualpa Yupanqui** was born **Héctor Roberto Chavero** in 1908, in Buenos Aires province. He took a Quechua-style name, often translated as *"the one who came from far lands to tell"*. He traveled the country on horseback and by foot, collecting songs, and wrote classics of the guitar. The main stage at Cosquín bears his name.

pages.title: The peña
pages.body: A **peña** is a folklore night: long tables, **empanadas** and **locro**, wine, and live music. There's no "audience". When a zamba or chacarera starts, people get up and dance between the tables, then sit back down and keep eating. A spontaneous version with friends and a guitar is a **guitarreada**.

pages.prompt: Match the word to what it is
pairs: folklore night with food and dancing

pages.title: Zamba vs chacarera
pages.body: **Zamba** (not the Brazilian samba!) is slow and romantic. Two dancers circle each other, never touching, waving a **pañuelo** (handkerchief), in a kind of flirting. **Chacarera**, tied to Santiago del Estero, is fast and happy: finger snaps, the man's **zapateo** (stomping footwork) and the woman's **zarandeo** (swirling her skirt).

pages.scenario: At a peña, the music goes slow and the couples on the floor pull out white handkerchiefs.
pages.prompt: What are they dancing?
pages.explain: The **pañuelo** is the trademark of the zamba. Slow, circling, never touching. If people are stomping and snapping, that's a chacarera.

pages.title: Nine moons in Cosquín
pages.body: Every January since 1961, the small town of **Cosquín**, in the Córdoba hills, hosts the **Festival Nacional de Folklore**. It runs nine nights, **las nueve lunas**. It happens in the **Plaza Próspero Molina**, and every night opens with the famous shout: **"¡Aquí Cosquín!"**

pages.prompt: You're at a peña and someone invites you to get up and dance a chacarera. You say yes:
pages.translation: Sure! But I don't know how to stomp.
pages.explain: **Dale** = sure, let's go. Nobody expects a foreigner to zapatear well. Getting up is what counts.

classes.title: Cumbia and cuarteto
classes.summary: The bailanta, a cumbia saint, and the tunga tunga from Córdoba

pages.title: The bailanta
pages.body: Rock fills stadiums, but **cumbia** fills the dance floor. Born in Colombia, it became deeply Argentine in the dance halls of the suburbs, the **bailantas**. They boomed in the 90s and never went away. At any wedding or birthday, at some point the DJ puts on cumbia and even your serious uncle starts moving. You don't have to like it. You just have to dance.

pages.title: Gilda, the cumbia saint
pages.body: **Gilda** (Miriam Bianchi) was a kindergarten teacher who became a cumbia star in her 30s, in a scene run by men. Her hit **"No me arrepiento de este amor"** is still sung everywhere. On September 7, 1996, her tour bus crashed on **Ruta 12**, in Entre Ríos. She was 34. People started asking her for miracles, and she became a **santa popular** (folk saint).

pages.statement: At the crash site on Ruta 12 there's a shrine to Gilda where people still leave offerings and ask for favors.
pages.explain: Yes, at kilometer 129. People ask for health, work or love, and leave thanks. On key dates thousands of people visit. The Church never made her a saint; the people did.

pages.title: Cumbia villera
pages.body: In the late 90s, with the economy collapsing, a rawer style was born in the poor neighborhoods: **cumbia villera**. Its big name is **Pablo Lescano**, whose band **Damas Gratis** started in 2000. The lyrics talk about the street, partying and the police. Critics say they glorify drugs and treat women badly. Fans say it's the honest voice of the barrio. Both debates are still alive.

pages.title: Cuarteto: Córdoba's heartbeat
pages.body: **Cuarteto** was born in **Córdoba** in 1943, with the **Cuarteto Leo**. Its pianist, **Leonor Marzano**, created the bouncy left-hand beat everybody calls **tunga tunga**. In December 2025, UNESCO declared cuarteto Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Its king is **La Mona Jiménez**, who has played packed weekly **bailes** for decades.

pages.title: El Potro
pages.body: **Rodrigo Bueno**, **el Potro** (*the colt*), took cuarteto from Córdoba to Buenos Aires and filled the **Luna Park** again and again. On June 24, 2000, after a show, he died in a car crash on the Buenos Aires–La Plata highway. He was 27. His songs, like **"Soy cordobés"** and **"Lo mejor del amor"**, are still party must-haves.

pages.prompt: Match the artist to their story

pages.scenario: You're at a wedding in Córdoba. At 3 a.m. the DJ switches to a fast beat with a bouncy piano, and everyone runs to the dance floor.
pages.prompt: What's probably playing?
pages.explain: In Córdoba, the late-night party is cuarteto. That bouncy piano is the **tunga tunga**. Refusing to dance is not really an option.

pages.prompt: Your friend is inviting you to a night of cumbia dancing:
pages.translation: Shall we go to the bailanta tonight?
pages.explain: The **bailanta** is the cumbia dance hall. A **peña** is folklore, and the **cancha** is the football stadium.

example.en: My dad loves cumbia.

vocabulary.en: folk saint (made by the people, not the Church)

example.en: Come on, come dance.
That song was a huge hit.

classes.title: Trap, RKT and Bizarrap
classes.summary: From freestyle battles in a park to the biggest stages in the world

pages.title: It started in a park
pages.body: From 2012 to 2017, on Sunday afternoons, kids met at **Parque Rivadavia**, in Caballito, for **El Quinto Escalón** (*the fifth step*): free rap battles on the park's steps. Rappers improvised rhymes against each other, **tirar freestyle**, and the crowd picked the winner. Names like **Duki**, **Trueno** and **Wos** came out of there. Today they fill stadiums.

pages.statement: Most of Argentina's big trap stars came up through expensive music schools.
pages.explain: Many of them started in free freestyle battles in parks and plazas, recorded on phones and shared on YouTube. The street was the school.

pages.title: The man in the cap
pages.body: **Bizarrap** (Gonzalo Conde, from Ramos Mejía) is a producer who never shows his face: always a cap and dark glasses. In his **BZRP Music Sessions**, a guest raps or sings over his beat, filmed in a small studio. **Nicki Nicole**'s session in 2019 launched her. **Shakira**'s, in January 2023, got about 63 million YouTube views in 24 hours and earned a pile of Guinness World Records.

pages.scenario: Your Argentine friend says: "¿Viste la nueva sesión de Biza?"
pages.prompt: What are they asking?
options: If you saw Bizarrap's new session
If you saw a new TV series
If you went to the gym
pages.explain: **Biza** is short for Bizarrap. When a new session drops, half the country listens that same day.

pages.title: The new stars
pages.body: In June 2024, **Duki** became the first Argentine to headline Real Madrid's **Bernabéu** stadium. In March 2024, **María Becerra**, who started as a YouTuber, became the first Argentine woman to headline **River**'s stadium, twice in a row. **Tini** Stoessel, once the star of Disney's *Violetta*, fills stadiums with pop. **Nicki Nicole**, from Rosario, mixes trap and R&B.

pages.title: RKT and the turreo
pages.body: **RKT** was born in the late 2000s, from DJs at a club called **Rescate** in San Martín, Buenos Aires province. It's reggaetón plus cumbia villera, with huge bass. **L-Gante** made it explode in 2020 with the viral **"L-Gante RKT"**. RKT parties are called **turreo**. Critics call the lyrics crude; fans say it's the sound of their barrio.

pages.prompt: Match the artist to the fact
pairs: first Argentine to headline the Bernabéu
first Argentine woman to headline River
producer who never shows his face

pages.prompt: Put these moments in order
items: The first El Quinto Escalón battle in Parque Rivadavia
Shakira's session with Bizarrap breaks records
pages.explain: 2012, 2019, 2020, 2023, 2024. A decade from park steps to Real Madrid's stadium.

pages.prompt: You just heard María Becerra's new song and you loved it.
pages.translation: What a banger! I can't stop listening to it.
pages.explain: **Temazo** = a great song. The **-azo** ending makes anything bigger and better.

pages.statement: If someone says a singer "la rompió", they mean she broke something on stage.
pages.explain: **La rompió** = she killed it, she was amazing. "María la rompió en River" is a compliment.

example.en: Come on, drop a freestyle.
The new session is out.

vocabulary.en: to kill it, to be amazing

example.en: Duki killed it.

vocabulary.note: Street slang. Fine among friends.

classes.title: Live: pogo, bengalas and misas
classes.summary: Why foreign bands leave Argentina a little shaken

pages.title: Recital, not concierto
pages.body: In Argentina you go to a **recital** or a **show**; **concierto** sounds a bit formal. At a big one, **campo** is the standing area on the pitch, **platea** is seats. The **telonero** is the opening act. And the crowd does not just listen: it sings *every* word, often louder than the band. Many foreign artists say it's one of the loudest crowds they've ever played to.

pages.scenario: Your friend texts you: "Tengo dos entradas para campo, ¿venís?"
pages.prompt: Where will you be?
options: In a seat up in the stands
Standing on the pitch, near the stage
pages.explain: **Campo** is the standing area on the field. Closer to the band, and closer to the pogo.

pages.title: Olé, olé, olé
pages.body: Between songs, the crowd sings a football-style chant with the artist's name: **"Olé, olé, olé, olé… Charly, Charly!"**. Foreigners get it too. When Paul McCartney plays Buenos Aires, the stadium chants his name like he's a football idol. The Rolling Stones even titled their 2016 Latin America documentary *Olé, Olé, Olé!*. Argentina has so many Stones fans they have a name: **rollingas**.

pages.prompt: The band walks off before the encore. What does the whole stadium shout?
pages.translation: One more, one more!
pages.explain: **¡Otro, otro!** is the Argentine way to ask for an encore. If that doesn't work, switch to "olé, olé" with the band's name.

pages.title: The pogo
pages.body: The **pogo** is jumping and bumping into each other in a big mass, usually near the stage. It looks like chaos, but there's an unwritten rule: **si alguien se cae, se lo levanta** (if someone falls, you pick them up). If you're not up for it, stay on the edges. **Pogear** is the verb.

pages.scenario: You're in the middle of the pogo at a rock show. The guy next to you trips and falls.
pages.prompt: What do you do?
options: Keep jumping, it's part of the pogo
Stop and help pick him up right away
pages.explain: The first rule of the pogo: whoever falls gets picked up, fast. People around you will do the same. Rough, but with a code.

pages.title: Misas ricoteras
pages.body: **Patricio Rey y sus Redonditos de Ricota**, **los Redondos**, led by the **Indio Solari**, never did much press. Their shows were called **misas** (masses) by fans, who traveled across the country for them. In the 90s, barrio rock like theirs, La Renga or Los Piojos, got the name **rock chabón**, with football-style banners, chants and flares.
pages.fun_fact: In March 2017, Indio Solari's solo show in Olavarría drew somewhere between 200,000 and 400,000 people, depending on who counted. Fans call the song "Ji ji ji" "the biggest pogo in the world".

pages.title: Bengalas and Cromañón
pages.body: **Bengalas** (flares) came to rock from the football stands. On December 30, 2004, at a Callejeros show at **República Cromañón**, a small club in Once, a flare set the ceiling on fire. The venue was overcrowded and an emergency exit was locked. **194 people died**, most of them young. It changed live music forever: much stricter controls, and a flare indoors is now unthinkable.

pages.statement: Since Cromañón, lighting a bengala inside a club in Argentina is seen as totally unacceptable.
pages.explain: Cromañón is a deep wound, and the families still hold memorials every December 30. You'll still see flares in some big outdoor shows, but inside a venue? Never.

pages.prompt: A typical Argentine recital night, in order
items: Queue outside for hours to get a good spot in campo
The telonero plays while the crowd fills up
The band comes out and everyone sings every word
The band leaves, the crowd chants "olé, olé" for more
They come back for the encore

example.en: Are you going to the gig on Saturday?

example.es: Yo pogeo solo en los temas rápidos.
example.en: I only mosh in the fast songs.

sections.title: Cómo hablamos
sections.summary: Vos, the "sh" sound, lunfardo and a lot of hands

classes.title: Vos, not tú
classes.summary: The little pronoun that makes you sound Argentine

pages.title: Goodbye, tú
pages.body: Your textbook taught you **tú**. Forget it here. In Argentina, "you" (informal) is **vos**: **vos sos** (you are), **vos tenés** (you have), **¿vos querés?** (do you want?). Say *tú tienes* in Buenos Aires and people will understand you perfectly, and instantly clock you as someone who learned Spanish from a book, or from Netflix.
pages.fun_fact: Uruguay and Paraguay use vos too, and so do parts of Central America.

pages.title: Just move the stress
pages.body: Good news: most vos forms are easy. In the present, take the infinitive, drop the **-r**, add **-s** and stress the end: **hablar → hablás**, **tener → tenés**, **venir → venís**. Commands are even shorter, just drop the **-r**: **¡vení!** (come!), **¡mirá!** (look!), **¡decime!** (tell me!). The one weird one: **ser → vos sos**.

pages.prompt: Match the tú form to its vos twin
pages.explain: Notice the vos forms never change the vowel inside: no *tienes*, no *quieres*. That's why kids here pick up verbs so fast.

pages.title: Why vos survived here
pages.body: Vos is old Spanish. In colonial times, **tú** took over in the rich centers, **Lima** and **Mexico City**, where viceroys and their courts kept up with Madrid's fashions. The Río de la Plata was a far-off, poor corner of the empire. Nobody bothered to update our pronoun, so vos just stayed. Being the backwater has its perks.

pages.statement: Argentine schools have always taught kids to use vos.
pages.explain: For a long time schools taught **tú**, even though nobody spoke it at home. In **1982** the Academia Argentina de Letras accepted vos as correct, educated Spanish, and classrooms slowly switched.

pages.title: No vosotros, and usted on standby
pages.body: Plural "you" is always **ustedes**. **Vosotros** is for Spain; here it only lives in the national anthem and old prayers. And **usted**? It's for respect and distance: an elderly neighbor, a doctor, a formal email. Still, people here drop into vos fast. A waiter your age will most likely vos you from the first word.

pages.scenario: You're at a kiosco. The guy behind the counter is about your age. You want to ask if he has change.
pages.prompt: What sounds most natural?
pages.explain: **¿Tenés cambio?** Short, vos, done. Also notice you don't even need to say *vos*: the **-és** ending already tells everyone who you mean.

pages.prompt: Your friend is late and texts you. What do you answer?
pages.translation: Sure, come whenever, no rush, I'll wait for you.
pages.explain: **Vení** is the vos command. *Ven* is tú, *venid* is vosotros: both sound foreign here.

pages.scenario: You're visiting your friend's grandmother, 85, for the first time. She offers you tea.
pages.prompt: How do you ask her if she wants help in the kitchen?
pages.explain: With an older person you've just met, **usted** is a safe bet: **¿Quiere que la ayude?** If she says "¡Tratame de vos, querido!", relax and switch.

example.en: And what are you up to?
Where are you from?
Do you want a coffee?
Tell me the truth.

vocabulary.note: Argentina never uses vosotros.

classes.title: Sho, che and the melody
classes.summary: The sound, the word and the tune that give a porteño away

pages.title: Sho me shamo
pages.body: The quickest way to spot a porteño: **y** and **ll** sound like English **"sh"**. **Yo** is "sho". **Calle** (street) is "cashe". **Pollo** (chicken) is "posho". **Me llamo** is "me shamo". Linguists call it **yeísmo rehilado**, the rest of the Spanish-speaking world calls it "the Argentine thing", and it's also heard across the river in Montevideo.

pages.title: Grandma says zh, you say sh
pages.body: It used to be softer: a buzzing **zh**, like the *s* in *measure*. Over the second half of the 20th century, younger porteños pushed it to a crisp **sh**, like *shoe*. Studies show young people, and especially women, lead the change. So a grandma in Palermo might say "zho" and her granddaughter "sho". Both are 100% porteño.

pages.statement: All Argentines pronounce "yo" as "sho".
pages.explain: It's the Buenos Aires region's trademark, and it spreads. But in the northeast, in places like **Corrientes** or **Misiones**, you'll often hear a softer *y*, and some people even say **ll** and **y** differently. Argentina is big.

pages.prompt: Which word here would a porteño say with a "sh" sound?
pages.translation: See you on Corrientes street.
pages.explain: **Calle** → "cashe". The double **ll** is the giveaway. *Casa* and *plaza* have no y or ll, so no sh.

pages.title: Che!
pages.body: **Che** is how you get someone's attention: "hey", "dude", "listen". **Che, ¿me pasás la sal?** **Che, ¿viste lo que pasó?** It's so typical of us that Ernesto Guevara's Cuban comrades nicknamed him **Che** because he said it all the time. Its best-known partner is **boludo** ("dude", or "idiot"), but that one has its own section.

pages.title: Where does che come from?
pages.body: Nobody knows for sure, and people love arguing about it. One theory: **Guaraní**, where *che* means "I" or "my". Another: **Mapudungun** (the Mapuche language), where *che* means "people". A third: the **Valencian** interjection for "hey". Every theory has fans and holes. Pick your favorite and defend it over a mate.

pages.prompt: Which of these is a real theory about where "che" comes from?
options: From Guaraní, where it means "I" or "my"
pages.explain: Guaraní is one of the favorites, along with Mapudungun and Valencian. "Ciao" gave us another word, though: **chau**, the everyday goodbye.

pages.title: Spanish with an Italian tune
pages.body: Foreigners often say porteños sound Italian. There's science behind it: CONICET researcher **Jorge Gurlekian** and **Laura Colantoni** (University of Toronto) compared Buenos Aires intonation with other languages and found it's closer to **Neapolitan** Italian than to anything else. The melody likely came with the huge wave of Italian immigrants around 1900. Before that, the city probably sounded more like Spain.

pages.statement: The Italian-sounding melody of Buenos Aires Spanish has been there since colonial times.
pages.explain: It's relatively recent. Researchers link it to the early 20th century, when Italians poured into the city. Their accents faded, but the tune stuck.

pages.scenario: You're walking with a friend and see an old classmate across the avenue.
pages.prompt: What's the most porteño way to call him?
pages.explain: **¡Che!** *Oye* sounds Spanish or Caribbean, and *oiga* is for a stranger you're about to complain to.

example.en: Hey, do you have the time?

vocabulary.note: From the Italian ciao.
Said "cashe" in Buenos Aires.

example.en: I'm Sofía, and you?
It was so cold, you know?

classes.title: Lunfardo
classes.summary: The street slang born in the conventillos

pages.title: A language made of immigrants
pages.body: Around 1900, Buenos Aires was packed with newcomers, mostly Italians and Spaniards, living side by side in **conventillos** (tenements). Out of that mix came **lunfardo**: a street vocabulary built from Italian dialects, Spanish slang, Portuguese and whatever else was lying around. The name itself probably comes from **lombardo**, someone from Lombardy, which back then had become slang for "thief".

pages.title: Police first, poets later
pages.body: The first people who wrote lunfardo down, in the late 1800s, were **police officers and journalists**, convinced it was the secret code of thieves. Turned out half the city talked like that. Then **tango** took it to the radio: **Mi noche triste** (1917), sung by Carlos Gardel, is considered the first tango-canción, a tango that tells a story, and its lyrics are packed with lunfardo. After that, there was no stopping it.

pages.title: The starter pack
pages.body: Words you'll hear today: **guita** (money), **mango** (a peso: *no tengo un mango* = I'm broke), **pibe** / **piba** (kid, guy, girl), **mina** (woman, a bit macho), **bondi** (bus), **laburo** (job, from Italian *lavoro*), **morfar** (to eat), **fiaca** (laziness). Pibe probably comes from Genoese *pivetto*, little boy.

pages.prompt: Match the lunfardo to its meaning

pages.title: Bondi: a word that took the tram
pages.body: In Brazil, trams are called **bonde**, from English **bond**. The story goes that early tram tickets were sold as "bonds". The word traveled south, and in Buenos Aires the tram became the **bondi**. When trams disappeared, the name jumped onto the **colectivo** (city bus). So every time you say "me tomo el bondi", you're quoting an English word by way of Brazilian Portuguese.

pages.scenario: A friend texts: "Estoy sin un mango, ¿morfamos en casa?"
pages.prompt: What's going on?
options: They're broke and suggest eating at home
They lost their phone and want to meet at home
pages.explain: **Sin un mango** = without a peso. **Morfar** = to eat. Bring a bottle of wine and you're the hero.

pages.title: The art of chamuyo
pages.body: **Chamuyo** is smooth talk: half truth, half invention, all charm. It comes from the Caló (Spanish Romani) *chamullar*, to talk. You **chamuyás** a date, a cop or your boss. Someone who does it too well is a **chamuyero**. And if someone's story sounds too good, just say **eso es puro chamuyo**: that's pure baloney.

pages.prompt: Your friend claims he almost got signed by Boca. What do you say?
pages.translation: Come on, that's pure baloney.
pages.explain: **Chamuyo** = sweet-talking nonsense. The other two would just mean "pure work" or "pure bus".

pages.prompt: Put lunfardo's life story in order
items: "Mi noche triste", the first tango-canción, full of lunfardo (1917)
José Gobello publishes "Lunfardía", a key study (1953)
The Academia Porteña del Lunfardo is founded (1962)
Buenos Aires starts celebrating the Día del Lunfardo on September 5 (2000)
pages.explain: The date of the Día del Lunfardo honors Gobello's book. Yes, slang has its own academy here, and its members take it very seriously.

pages.statement: Lunfardo is an old tango thing that nobody really uses anymore.
pages.explain: Some words aged (nobody says **percanta** for woman anymore), but **guita**, **laburo**, **pibe** and **bondi** are everyday Spanish here, from kids to newsreaders.

example.en: I don't have enough money.
I'm broke.

vocabulary.note: Piba for a girl. Used for adults too.
Very casual, can sound a bit macho.

example.en: I'm taking the bus.

example.es: La estaba chamuyando toda la noche.
example.en: He was chatting her up all night.

classes.title: Vesre, re and posta
classes.summary: Words backwards, words turned up, and the truth

pages.title: Al vesre
pages.body: Porteños like to flip words around. Swap the syllables of **revés** (backwards) and you get **vesre**: the name of the game is itself vesre. **Café** becomes **feca**, **mujer** becomes **jermu**, **tango** becomes **gotán**. It's playful, it's a bit of a wink, and it came up along with lunfardo on the streets and in tango lyrics.

pages.prompt: Flip them back: match the vesre to the original
pages.explain: Some are old-fashioned now (**gotán**, **jermu**), but **garpar** (to pay) and **telo** are used every day.

pages.title: Careful with telo
pages.body: A **telo** is not just any hotel. It's a **hotel alojamiento**: rooms by the hour, discreet entrance, for couples who want privacy. With so many people living with their parents into their twenties, telos are a normal, even cheerful, part of city life. For your holiday hotel, just say **hotel**.

pages.scenario: At a party you tell a new friend: "Me estoy quedando en un telo re lindo en Palermo." Everyone bursts out laughing.
pages.prompt: Why?
options: You just said you're living in a love hotel
pages.explain: **Telo** = love hotel, rented by the hour. For your stay, say **hotel**, or **hostel** if you're a backpacker. Great story for the rest of the night, though.

pages.title: Re: the volume knob
pages.body: Want to say "very"? Stick **re** in front: **re lindo** (really nice), **re lejos** (super far), **re bien**. Need more? **Recontra**: **recontra cansado**, dead tired. It even works alone as an answer: **—¿Te gustó? —¡Re!** (Did you like it? Totally!) Once you start, you'll never say *muy* again.

pages.prompt: Your friend asks how the concert was. It was amazing.
pages.translation: It was really good!
pages.explain: **Re bueno** is the natural way. *Mucho bueno* is just wrong, and *tan bueno* usually sets up more: *tan bueno que…*

pages.title: Posta
pages.body: **Posta** means "for real". **¿Posta?** = Really? Seriously? **Te lo digo posta** = I'm telling you straight. **La posta** is the real info, the inside story. The word comes from Italian.

pages.statement: If a friend answers your news with "¿Posta?", they're asking if it's true or just joking.
pages.explain: **¿Posta?** = Seriously? It's the Argentine *¿en serio?*, usually with raised eyebrows.

pages.prompt: From calm to over-the-top: order these
pages.explain: **Muy** is fine, **re** is how people actually talk, and **recontra** is for when you really, really mean it.

example.en: Shall we grab a coffee?

vocabulary.note: Playful. Café is still the normal word.

example.en: Who's paying?
It's really far.
Are you really leaving?

vocabulary.en: the real deal, the inside info

classes.title: Hands and texts
classes.summary: Gestures you'll see and shortcuts you'll read

pages.title: Talking with your hands
pages.body: Porteños don't just speak, they perform. Hands go up, fingers pinch, wrists shake. Part of it is the Italian heritage, part of it is plain passion. Watch two friends arguing about football from across the street: you'll get the gist without hearing a word. Learn a few gestures and you'll understand half the conversation before your Spanish catches up.

pages.title: The montoncito
pages.body: Fingertips pinched together pointing up, wrist bobbing up and down: that's the **montoncito** (little pile). It means **¿qué te pasa?** or **¿qué querés?**, "what's your problem?", from friendly to threatening depending on the face. Now keep the wrist still and open and close the fingers: that one means someone's scared (**tiene miedo**).
pages.fun_fact: In 2020 the gesture got its own emoji: 🤌, officially "pinched fingers".

pages.scenario: Someone cuts in front of you in the bondi line. The lady behind you looks at him, fingers pinched, shaking her wrist.
pages.prompt: What is she telling him?
pages.explain: The bobbing **montoncito** = **¿qué te pasa?** Here, pure indignation. He'll probably move.

pages.title: Three more to know
pages.body: Open hand, palm down, rocking side to side: **más o menos**, so-so. Back of your fingers brushed forward under your chin: **ni idea**, no clue. Index finger pulling down your lower eyelid: **ojo**, careful, keep an eye out. Throw in a shrug and you can survive a whole conversation.

pages.prompt: Match the gesture to what it means
pairs: Flat hand rocking side to side
Back of fingers flicked under the chin
Finger pulling down the lower eyelid

pages.title: The group chat
pages.body: In a WhatsApp group you'll see: **q onda** (what's up, from **¿qué onda?**), **bue** (well, OK… with a sigh), **ntp** (**no te preocupes**, don't worry), **tqm** (**te quiero mucho**, love you), **xq** (**porque**, because), **dsp** (**después**, later). And a strict rule: nobody writes a full sentence when three letters will do.

pages.prompt: Decode the texts

pages.title: Ni ahí and nada que ver
pages.body: Two phrases that do a lot of work. **Ni ahí** = not at all, no way: **¿Te gusta el reggaetón? —Ni ahí.** **Nada que ver** = that's got nothing to do with it, or totally off: **¿Estás enojado? —No, nada que ver.** Say them with a little eye roll and you'll sound like you grew up in Caballito.

pages.prompt: A friend asks if you're mad that she canceled. You're really not.
pages.translation: No, not at all, don't worry.
pages.explain: **Nada que ver** = not at all, that's not it. Add **tranqui** (relax) and she'll believe you.

pages.scenario: You suggest going for a run at 7 a.m. on Sunday. Your friend replies: "bue".
pages.prompt: How excited are they?
options: Going along with it, not happy about it
pages.explain: **Bue** is **bueno** with a sigh: fine, whatever, if we must. Expect them to show up late.

vocabulary.en: what's wrong with you?, what's your problem?

example.es: Ojo con el celular en el subte.
example.en: Watch your phone on the subway.
What's up, all good?

classes.title: Everyday expressions
classes.summary: The phrases you'll hear before lunch on any given day

pages.title: Idioms, Argentine style
pages.body: A **dicho** is a saying or expression. Argentines talk in them constantly, and they rarely mean what the words say. Learn the words alone and you'll understand every word of a sentence, and still miss the point. So let's learn the phrases whole, the way a porteño says them.
pages.fun_fact: Many of these are also used in Uruguay: it's the Río de la Plata, not just Buenos Aires.

pages.title: The penny drops
pages.body: **Me cayó la ficha** = 'the penny dropped', 'I finally got it'. It comes from old public phones that ran on **fichas** (tokens): the call only went through when the token fell. The opposite: **no le cae la ficha** = 'he still doesn't get it'.

pages.title: In the oven
pages.body: **Estar al horno** = 'to be in the oven', i.e. in big trouble. Exam tomorrow, nothing studied? **Estoy al horno.** Your team loses 3–0 at half time? **Estamos al horno.** When things are hopeless but it's also a little funny, add **con papas**: **al horno con papas**, like a roast with potatoes.

pages.scenario: Your friend explains a joke for the third time. Suddenly you laugh.
pages.prompt: What do you say?
pages.explain: **Me cayó la ficha** = 'Now I get it!'. The token finally dropped.

pages.title: Pulling your hair
pages.body: **Tomar el pelo** = 'to pull someone's leg' (literally 'to take the hair'). **¿Me estás tomando el pelo?** = 'Are you kidding me?'. And when someone needs to get their act together: **ponete las pilas** = 'put your batteries in', i.e. wake up, get going.

pages.prompt: Your roommate has been on the couch all week and exams start Monday.
pages.translation: Hey, get your act together.
pages.explain: **Ponerse las pilas** = recharge and get to work.

pages.title: Drags and vibes
pages.body: **¡Qué garrón!** = 'What a drag!': a cancelled plan, a rainy Saturday, a two-hour line at the bank. The opposite feeling is **buena onda** (good vibes, nice): **Tu hermana es re buena onda** = 'Your sister is really nice'. And **mala onda** is bad vibes, or a person who's unfriendly.

pages.statement: If an Argentine says 'estoy al horno', they're probably cooking.
pages.explain: They're in trouble. The only thing roasting is them.

classes.title: Más perdido que turco en la neblina
classes.summary: The comparisons Argentines use to exaggerate everything

pages.title: More X than Y
pages.body: Why say 'very lost' when you can say **más perdido que turco en la neblina**: 'more lost than a Turk in the fog'? Argentines love these **más … que …** comparisons. They're vivid, a bit absurd, and everyone knows them by heart. Use one at the right moment and you'll get a laugh and a look of respect.
pages.fun_fact: 'Turco' was the loose name given to immigrants from the Ottoman Empire: Syrians, Lebanese, Armenians and more.

pages.title: Lost, long and boring
pages.body: **Más perdido que turco en la neblina**: totally lost, or clueless. **Más largo que esperanza de pobre**: 'longer than a poor man's hope', for a line, a meeting or a week that never ends. **Más aburrido que chupar un clavo**: 'more boring than sucking a nail'.

pages.scenario: You've been waiting at the immigration office for four hours. Your number still isn't up.
pages.prompt: How would you describe the wait?
options: Más largo que esperanza de pobre
Más perdido que turco en la neblina
pages.explain: Endless = **más largo que esperanza de pobre**. It also works for anything that drags on.

pages.title: Fakes and pests
pages.body: **Más trucho que billete de tres pesos**: 'faker than a three-peso bill' (**trucho** = fake, dodgy). **Más pesado que collar de melones**: 'heavier than a necklace of melons', for someone who's a real pain. And a happy one: **más contento que perro con dos colas**, 'happier than a dog with two tails'.

pages.prompt: A guy on the street is selling 'original' Messi shirts for almost nothing.
pages.text: Esa camiseta es más trucha que billete de tres ___.
pages.translation: That shirt is as fake as a three-peso bill.
pages.explain: There's no such thing as a three-peso bill, so it's obviously **trucho**.

pages.title: Round and round
pages.body: Someone who can't make a simple decision **tiene más vueltas que una calesita**: 'has more turns than a merry-go-round'. And someone who thinks they're irresistible **se cree la última Coca-Cola del desierto**: 'thinks they're the last Coke in the desert'.

pages.prompt: What do you say about her?

pages.explain: Pure joy = a dog with two tails to wag.

pages.explain: Fake bills, fake shirts, a dodgy deal: all **trucho**. Very common word.

classes.title: Grandma's refranes
classes.summary: The old sayings every abuela has ready for any occasion

pages.title: What's a refrán?
pages.body: A **refrán** is a proverb: a short, fixed sentence with a lesson inside. Most came from Spain and are known all over the Spanish-speaking world, but Argentines tweak them with their own **vos** verbs and details. Your abuela will quote one before you finish telling her your problem.

pages.title: Burned by milk
pages.body: The English 'once bitten, twice shy' becomes **el que se quema con leche, ve una vaca y llora**: 'whoever gets burned by milk cries when they see a cow'. Another classic: **no hay mal que por bien no venga**, 'every cloud has a silver lining' (there's no bad thing that doesn't bring something good).

pages.scenario: After a terrible breakup, your friend refuses to even go on a first date.
pages.prompt: Which refrán fits?
options: El que se quema con leche, ve una vaca y llora
Al que madruga, Dios lo ayuda
Más vale pájaro en mano que cien volando
pages.explain: Burned once, now scared of everything that looks similar.

pages.title: Birds and horses
pages.body: **Más vale pájaro en mano que cien volando**: 'a bird in the hand is worth a hundred flying' (in English, only two in the bush). **A caballo regalado no se le miran los dientes**: 'don't look a gift horse in the mouth'. And **al que madruga, Dios lo ayuda**: 'God helps those who get up early'.

pages.prompt: Put the refrán back together

pages.title: Said and done
pages.body: **Del dicho al hecho hay mucho trecho**: 'from saying to doing is a long way', easy to promise, hard to deliver. **Camarón que se duerme se lo lleva la corriente**: 'the shrimp that falls asleep gets carried away by the current', snooze and you lose. **Ojos que no ven, corazón que no siente**: what you don't know can't hurt you.

pages.prompt: Match the refrán to its English cousin
pairs: A caballo regalado no se le miran los dientes

pages.prompt: Your friend promises, again, that he'll start the gym on Monday.
pages.text: Del dicho al ___ hay mucho trecho.
pages.translation: Easier said than done.
pages.explain: **Dicho** (said) and **hecho** (done) rhyme with **trecho** (a stretch of road). That's why it sticks.

pages.statement: Refranes are only understood by old people.
pages.explain: Everyone knows them. Young people often quote them half-jokingly, or just say the first half and let you finish it.
