classes.title: Argentine philosophy in six sentences
classes.summary: The maxims that explain how the country sees itself

pages.title: A country in sayings
pages.body: Some sayings aren't just proverbs: they're a worldview. Crisis after crisis, Argentines built a set of maxims that are part resignation, part humour, part survival guide. Hear them and you'll understand a lot about how people here think. Take them with a pinch of salt: they're often said with a wink.

pages.title: Crying and cheating
pages.body: **El que no llora, no mama**: 'the baby who doesn't cry doesn't get fed', if you don't complain, you get nothing. **Hecha la ley, hecha la trampa**: 'as soon as a law is made, so is the way around it'. Both are said with a shrug, about bureaucracy, taxes and life in general.

pages.scenario: The bank keeps ignoring your complaint. Your Argentine friend tells you to call every day and make noise.
pages.prompt: Which saying is she following?
options: El que no llora, no mama
Hecha la ley, hecha la trampa
pages.explain: Squeaky wheel gets the grease. Complain, insist, and you'll get it.

pages.title: The vivo and the gil
pages.body: Remember the **vivo** (sharp) and the **gil** (sucker)? A famously cynical maxim: **el vivo vive del gil, y el gil de su trabajo**, 'the sharp one lives off the sucker, and the sucker off his work'. It's part of **viveza criolla**, the 'native cunning' Argentines both joke about and criticise in themselves.
pages.fun_fact: Plenty of Argentines blame viveza criolla for the country's problems. It's a joke and a confession at the same time.

pages.statement: Argentines say 'el vivo vive del gil' as a proud national motto.
pages.explain: It's cynical and self-critical, said with irony. Admiring the **vivo** out loud would make most people wince.

pages.title: Wire and hope
pages.body: **Atado con alambre**: 'tied up with wire', anything held together by a quick, improvised fix. A car, a plan, sometimes the whole economy. And for hard times: **siempre que llovió, paró**, 'every time it rained, it stopped'. When luck saves the day at the last second, someone will say **Dios es argentino**: God is Argentine.

pages.prompt: Your friend is devastated after losing her job. You want to comfort her.
pages.translation: Relax, it always stops raining eventually.
pages.explain: Hard times pass. It's one of the kindest things you can say.

pages.prompt: Match the maxim to the situation
pairs: The fridge door is held shut with a belt
A goal in the 94th minute saves the team
Hecha la ley, hecha la trampa
A new tax, and everyone already knows how to dodge it
Comforting a friend after a bad year

pages.scenario: Your landlord repairs the leaking pipe with tape and a plastic bag. He says it's 'perfect'.
pages.prompt: How would your Argentine friend describe it?
pages.explain: A fix that works for now, and nobody knows for how long: **atado con alambre**.

sections.title: Puteadas
sections.summary: Argentine swearing: what it means, and when to keep your mouth shut

classes.title: Boludo, the word that does everything
classes.summary: Greeting, insult, punctuation: one word, many jobs

pages.title: Welcome to the puteadas
pages.body: Grab a mate. In Argentina a **puteada** is a swear or an insult, and **putear** is to swear at someone (or at the universe). Argentines swear a lot, and often with love. This section teaches you to *understand* them, and, more importantly, when *not* to use them.
pages.fun_fact: Many visitors say they hear more swearing in a Buenos Aires café than in most bars back home.

pages.title: Boludo
pages.body: **Boludo** (**boluda** for a woman) literally means 'big-balled', i.e. an idiot. But between friends it softened into 'dude' or 'mate'. **¿Qué hacés, boludo?** is just 'What's up, man?'. Same word, said slowly with a stare, is still an insult: 'you idiot'. Tone and relationship decide everything.
pages.fun_fact: Some porteños use it so often it's basically a comma: 'Fui al súper, boludo, y no había nada, boludo.'

pages.scenario: Your friend Nico sees you at the bar, grins and shouts: '¡Boludo! ¿Qué hacés acá?'
pages.prompt: Is Nico insulting you?
options: No, he's happy to see you
pages.explain: Warm tone plus a friend = **boludo** means 'dude'. He's just surprised to see you there.

pages.scenario: Your brand-new boss, on your first day, says: 'Che, boludo, pasame eso.'
pages.prompt: What's going on?
options: He's being overly casual: odd, but probably not an insult
It's the formal way to talk at work
pages.explain: Probably not an insult: some people use **boludo** with anyone. But it's very casual for a boss, and it's never the 'formal' option. Don't say it back until you know him well.

pages.title: Pelotudo: the upgrade
pages.body: **Pelotudo** comes from **pelotas** (balls, again) and means 'idiot' too, but stronger. It's rarely affectionate. **¡Qué pelotudo!** = 'What an idiot!'. A silly or trivial thing is a **boludez** or **pelotudez**: 'Es una boludez' = 'It's nothing / it's a dumb little thing'.

pages.statement: Pelotudo is the friendly, softer version of boludo.
pages.explain: It's the other way around. **Boludo** can be friendly; **pelotudo** almost always stings.

pages.prompt: Your friend apologizes for spilling a bit of mate. How do you say 'Don't worry, it's nothing'?
pages.translation: Relax, it's nothing.
pages.explain: **Boludez** = a trivial thing. Friendly and harmless.

pages.scenario: A stranger bumps into you on the subte and you say '¡Boludo!' with a frown.
pages.prompt: How will he hear it?
pages.explain: No friendship, angry tone: it's an insult. The word didn't change; the context did.

example.en: What's up, dude?
Girl, you won't believe what happened!
What an idiot!
It's nothing.
He swore at me in the street.

classes.title: Gil, forro, chanta: the cast of characters
classes.summary: The people Argentines love to complain about

pages.title: The gil
pages.body: A **gil** is a sucker: naive, easy to fool. It's an old lunfardo word from tango days, when the **gil** was the one who got scammed and the **vivo** was the sharp guy. **No seas gil** = 'Don't be a sucker'. Rude, but mild.
pages.fun_fact: Tango lyrics are full of giles who got their heart broken.

pages.title: The chanta
pages.body: A **chanta** is a bullshitter: someone who brags, promises and never delivers. The plumber who says 'mañana vengo' for three weeks? **Chanta**. The guy who claims he played in the Primera? **Chanta**. It's short for **chantapufi**, from a Genoese word for someone who doesn't pay his debts.

pages.title: The forro
pages.body: **Forro** literally means 'lining' and is also slang for condom. Called at a person, it means a jerk: someone mean, disloyal or selfish. **Sos un forro** = 'You're such a jerk'. It hurts more than **boludo** because it's about character, not brains.

pages.prompt: Match the character to who they are

pages.scenario: A taxi driver charges you triple because you're a tourist, and you paid.
pages.prompt: What would your Argentine friend call you, lovingly?
pages.explain: You got fooled, so you're the **gil**. The taxi driver is the **chanta** (or the **forro**).

pages.title: The pests
pages.body: Someone who won't stop bugging you is a **hinchapelotas** or **rompebolas**: literally 'ball-swelling' and 'ball-breaking'. Pain in the neck. **Pajero** literally means 'wanker'; among friends it usually means lazy or useless: **No seas pajero, ayudame** = 'Don't be lazy, help me'. Crude, so keep it among friends.

pages.statement: Calling your friend a 'hinchapelotas' because he texts you 40 times a day is a fair use of the word.
pages.explain: Exactly the right use. Between friends it's a jokey complaint, not a war.

pages.prompt: Your roommate is on the couch while you carry all the groceries.
pages.translation: Don't be lazy, help me!
pages.explain: **Pajero** here = lazy. A **chanta** lies, a **gil** gets fooled.

pages.scenario: Your friend promised to help you move, didn't show up, and posted beach pics that same day.
pages.prompt: Which word fits him best?
pages.explain: Disloyal and selfish: that's a **forro**. A **boludez** is a trivial thing, not a person.

example.en: Don't be a sucker.
That plumber is all talk.
You're such a jerk.
You're such a pain!

vocabulary.en: wanker; among friends, lazy or useless

example.en: Don't be lazy, help me.

vocabulary.en: sharp, street-smart (the opposite of a gil)

classes.title: La puta madre: pure frustration
classes.summary: The exclamations for when everything goes wrong

pages.title: Swearing at the universe
pages.body: Stub your toe, miss the bus, see the inflation numbers: **¡La puta madre!** Nobody's mother is involved; it's just 'Damn it!'. It goes up in levels: **la puta que lo parió** ('the whore who gave birth to it') and the maximum, **la re puta que lo parió**. The **re** means 'really, super'.
pages.fun_fact: People shorten it to just 'La puta…' with a long, tired sigh.

pages.title: The heavy one
pages.body: **¡La concha de tu madre!** is very vulgar (**concha** is vulgar slang for female genitals). Shouted at nobody, after dropping your phone in the toilet, it's frustration. Aimed at a person, it's a serious insult. Fun variant: **la concha de la lora** ('the parrot's...'), pure frustration, no target.

pages.prompt: Order these from mildest to strongest
pages.explain: The euphemism is softest, and aiming a vulgar phrase *at a person* is the strongest of all.

pages.title: Dismissals
pages.body: **¡Andá a cagar!** literally 'go take a shit', means 'get lost'. But between friends it's often disbelief: 'No way!' or 'Shut up!'. And **me chupa un huevo** ('it sucks me an egg', with egg = testicle) means 'I don't give a damn', like **me importa un carajo** (or **tres carajos**). Deluxe version: **me chupa un huevo y la mitad del otro**.

pages.scenario: You tell your friend you met Messi at the airport. She laughs and says: '¡Andá a cagar!'
pages.prompt: What does she mean?
pages.explain: Laughing + amazing news = disbelief. Same words, said cold, would mean 'get lost'.

pages.prompt: Your coworker asks if you care who wins the reality show. You really don't.
pages.translation: I don't give a damn.
pages.explain: **Me chupa un huevo** = I couldn't care less. Crude, so coworkers only if you're close.

pages.title: The family-friendly versions
pages.body: Around kids or grandparents? Swap in a euphemism. **¡Miércoles!** ('Wednesday!') stands in for **mierda** (shit). **¡Pucha!** or **¡La pucha!** replaces **la puta**. **Me importa un pito** ('I don't care a whistle') is the tamer cousin of the egg one. Same frustration, no scandal.

pages.prompt: Match the polite version to the one it's hiding
pages.explain: Euphemisms sound like the real thing, so everyone knows what you meant, but nobody's offended.

pages.statement: When someone shouts '¡La puta madre!' after missing the bus, they're insulting someone's mother.
pages.explain: It's an exclamation, like 'Damn it!'. No mothers were harmed.

example.en: Damn it, I missed the bus!

vocabulary.es: la re puta que lo parió

vocabulary.en: very vulgar: frustration, or a serious insult at someone
vocabulary.note: Never aim it at a person unless you want a fight.

example.en: You met Messi? No way!
Darn, I dropped it!

vocabulary.note: Milder than 'me chupa un huevo' or 'me importa un carajo', but still not for a job interview.

classes.title: Reading the room
classes.summary: The stadium, the traffic, and your girlfriend's grandma

pages.title: At the cancha
pages.body: The football stadium (**la cancha**) is where swearing becomes a sport. The referee (**el referí**) gets **¡Cobrá, la concha de tu madre!** ('Make the call!'), and a slow striker hears **¡Dale, pelotudo!**. Warning: many stadium chants include slurs about gays, other nationalities and so on. We skip those, and so should you.
pages.fun_fact: The ref is insulted so often that some fans say it's part of the ticket price.

pages.statement: Singing along to every stadium chant is fine, since everyone else is doing it.
pages.explain: Lots of chants are homophobic or racist, and there's growing pushback against them. Cheer, swear at the ref, but skip the slurs.

pages.title: Behind the wheel
pages.body: Buenos Aires traffic turns saints into sailors. The light turns green and someone honks: **¡Dale, boludo!** ('Come on, idiot!'). Somebody cuts you off: **¡Aprendé a manejar!** ('Learn to drive!') or **¿Quién te dio el registro?** ('Who gave you a license?'). Usually it's just venting. Hand gestures can escalate things, so keep yours on the wheel.

pages.prompt: The light turned green five seconds ago and the car in front hasn't moved.
pages.translation: Come on, idiot!
pages.explain: Classic traffic venting. Said to a stranger in a car, **boludo** is an insult, but a very routine one.

pages.title: The abuela test
pages.body: Before you swear, ask: would I say this in front of my girlfriend's grandma? With close friends, **boludo**, **la puta madre** and **andá a cagar** are totally normal. With your boss, your in-laws, a cop or a stranger? Go polite: **¡pucha!**, **¡miércoles!** Swearing badly makes you sound rude; swearing well makes you sound local.

pages.scenario: Sunday lunch with your girlfriend's family. You burn your tongue on the ravioles.
pages.prompt: What do you say?
pages.explain: **La pucha** says 'ouch, darn' without making the abuela drop her fork.

pages.scenario: You're watching the match at a bar with your friends and your team misses a penalty.
pages.prompt: Which reaction fits in?
pages.explain: At a bar with friends during football, full swearing is expected. 'Oh dear' would get you strange looks.

pages.prompt: Order from 'swear freely' to 'keep it clean'
items: Your best friends at the cancha
pages.explain: The closer and more relaxed the relationship, the more puteadas are allowed.

pages.prompt: Match the place to the classic puteada

example.es: Vamos a la cancha el domingo.
example.en: We're going to the game on Sunday.

vocabulary.en: make the call! (shouted at the ref)

example.en: Who gave you a license?
Come on, it's green!

sections.title: Costumbres
sections.summary: Kisses, late arrivals, long goodbyes and a very full calendar

classes.title: Hello, with a kiss
classes.summary: One kiss, everybody, every time

pages.title: One kiss. Just one.
pages.body: In Argentina you say hi with **un beso**: one kiss, cheek to cheek, usually on the right side, with a little kissing sound. Not two like in Spain, not three. Friends, family, your friend's cousin you just met, the new guy at work: all get **un beso**. A handshake with someone your own age at a party can feel a bit cold.

pages.statement: Two Argentine men who are friends will usually greet each other with a handshake, never a kiss.
pages.explain: Men kiss too: friends, brothers, fathers and sons, teammates. It became more and more common over the last decades, and today it's the norm, especially among younger men. A kiss plus a pat on the back is the classic combo.

pages.title: Saludar a todos
pages.body: Arrive at a party with twelve people and you **saludás a todos**: you go around and kiss every single one, even the ones you don't know. A general "¡hola!" from the door comes across as unfriendly. And yes, you do it again when you leave. Budget five minutes for it, both ways.

pages.scenario: You get to a friend's birthday. Fifteen people are already sitting around the table, most of them strangers.
pages.prompt: What do you do?
options: Wave at everyone from the door and sit down
Go around and give each person a kiss
Shake hands with the men, kiss the women
pages.explain: Around the table, one by one, a kiss each. Say your name if they don't know you: "Hola, soy Sam". It's slow, and nobody minds.

pages.title: When it's a handshake
pages.body: The kiss rules social life, but not everything. A very formal first meeting, a job interview in a big company, an older official: often a handshake first. Watch what the other person does and copy them. A lot of the time the second meeting is already a kiss. When in doubt, lean in slowly and let them decide.

pages.title: ¿Todo bien?
pages.body: The greeting that follows the kiss is not a real question. **¿Todo bien?** (all good?), **¿Cómo andás?** (how's it going?), **¿Qué hacés?** (literally "what are you doing?", really just "hi"). The answer is short: **Todo bien, ¿vos?** Nobody expects a report on your week. That comes later, with a mate.

pages.prompt: A friend kisses you hello and says "¿Todo bien?". Answer the Argentine way.
pages.translation: All good, you?
pages.explain: Argentines use **vos**, not *tú*. And bouncing the question back is the polite part.

pages.scenario: A neighbor you barely know passes you in the hallway and says: "¿Qué hacés?"
pages.prompt: What is she asking?
options: What you're doing right now, in detail
pages.explain: **¿Qué hacés?** is a hello. "Bien, ¿vos?" is plenty. Explaining that you're taking out the trash is optional.

pages.prompt: Match the greeting to what it really means
pairs: Greet every person in the room

example.en: I'll greet you with a kiss.

vocabulary.note: Also how people sign off a message: "Beso" or "Besos".

vocabulary.en: to greet, to say hi or bye

example.es: Andá a saludar a tu tía.
example.en: Go say hi to your aunt.
—All good? —All good, you?

vocabulary.note: A greeting, not a real question.

example.es: Me dio un beso en el cachete.
example.en: She kissed me on the cheek.
Bye, see you.

classes.title: Argentine time
classes.summary: Late arrivals, loose plans and goodbyes that never end

pages.title: Nine means nine thirty
pages.body: Invited to a dinner **a las nueve**? Nobody expects you at nine. Showing up 20 or 30 minutes late to a party or a dinner at someone's house is normal, even polite: the host is probably still in the shower. Dinner itself is late, often around ten. Arriving early is the real faux pas.
pages.fun_fact: Surveys on punctuality keep finding the same thing: for plenty of Argentines, you're not really late until it's been half an hour.

pages.statement: Arriving 30 minutes late to a work meeting or a university class is fine, just like with a party.
pages.explain: The flexible clock is for social life. Meetings, classes, the doctor, a flight: be on time, or at least text. Ten minutes is forgiven; thirty is a problem.

pages.title: Ya salgo
pages.body: Learn to decode the texts. **Ya salgo** (I'm leaving now) often means "I'm about to get in the shower". **Estoy saliendo** (I'm heading out) means "soon, ish". **Llego en cinco** (I'll be there in five) means fifteen. Nobody is lying, exactly. It's more like a shared estimate everyone knows how to read.

pages.scenario: Your friend texts "ya salgo" at 21:00. You live 20 minutes apart.
pages.prompt: When do you realistically expect her?
pages.explain: **Ya salgo** has a little padding built in. Order a drink, relax.

pages.title: Traé algo para tomar
pages.body: Never show up empty-handed. The host will say **no traigas nada** (don't bring anything). Bring something anyway. Often they'll ask directly: **traé algo para tomar** (bring something to drink): wine, beer, a soda. Other safe bets: something sweet for dessert, or a tub of **helado** from the heladería, sold by weight, a kilo being the classic.

pages.prompt: Your friend is hosting and you ask what to bring. She answers:
pages.text: Traé algo para ___, que la comida la pongo yo.
pages.translation: Bring something to drink, I've got the food covered.
pages.explain: Argentines **toman**, they don't *beben*. "Algo para tomar" means drinks, from wine to Coca-Cola.

pages.title: Juntada and vamos viendo
pages.body: A **juntada** is any get-together with friends. Plans for one live in a WhatsApp group, full of **audios** (voice notes), some long enough to be a podcast. The key phrase: **vamos viendo** (let's see how it goes). It means the plan is alive but nothing is fixed. Don't book a table for eight based on a "vamos viendo".
pages.fun_fact: Leaving someone on read is **clavar el visto**, literally "nailing the seen".

pages.title: The endless goodbye
pages.body: Leaving takes a while. You announce **bueno, me voy yendo** (well, I'm getting going), then someone serves another round, then you kiss everyone goodbye, then you chat at the door for twenty minutes. Slipping out without saying goodbye is **irse a la francesa** (leaving French-style), and people notice.

pages.prompt: Leave a party, Argentine style
items: Kiss everyone goodbye, one by one
pages.explain: From announcement to exit, half an hour is normal. Add it to your plans.

pages.prompt: Match the phrase to what it really means

example.es: El sábado hay juntada en lo de Caro.
example.en: There's a get-together at Caro's on Saturday.
—Are you coming Friday? —We'll see.
I'll send you a voice note.
He left me on read.

classes.title: Going out
classes.summary: The previa, the boliche and breakfast at sunrise

pages.title: The night starts late
pages.body: If you're used to going out at nine, recalibrate. In Buenos Aires dinner is around ten, the bar is at midnight, and the **boliche** (nightclub) opens around 1 a.m. Most people walk in between two and three. Going home at six, with the sun coming up, is a normal Saturday, not a wild one.

pages.title: La previa
pages.body: Before the boliche comes **la previa**: friends meet at someone's place to drink, eat something and warm up. It's cheaper than drinking at the club, and honestly it's often the best part of the night. It usually starts around midnight. Ask **¿dónde es la previa?** (where's the pregame?) and you're part of the plan.
pages.fun_fact: Football fans use the same word for the hours before a match.

pages.scenario: Your friends say: "Previa en lo de Tomi, después vamos al boliche." You show up at Tomi's at 21:00.
pages.prompt: What do you find?
options: Tomi in his pajamas, eating dinner
Everyone already leaving for the club
pages.explain: At nine the night hasn't started. The previa gets going around midnight, and you might leave for the boliche at two.

pages.statement: Boliches in Buenos Aires usually open their doors around 9 or 10 p.m.
pages.explain: More like 1 a.m., and they fill up from two. Show up at eleven and you'll dance alone with the bartender.

pages.prompt: A classic Saturday night, in order
items: La previa at a friend's place
Walk into the boliche, around two
pages.explain: Ending the night with coffee and **medialunas** (croissants) in a bar that's just opening is a porteño classic.

pages.title: The after
pages.body: For some, six a.m. isn't the end. An **after** is a party that keeps going after the boliche closes, at a house or a place that opens in the morning. Everyone else goes for **un café con medialunas** and heads home to sleep until lunch. Sunday afternoon exists mainly for recovery, often with a mate.

pages.prompt: It's Saturday, and you want to know where your friends are meeting before the club.
pages.translation: Where's the pregame?
pages.explain: The **previa** comes before. The **sobremesa** is the long chat after a meal, and the **cancha** is the football ground.

pages.prompt: Match the night word to its meaning

example.en: Which club are we going to?
We'll do pregame at my place.
Are you going out tonight?

classes.title: No filter
classes.summary: Money talk, body comments and the viveza criolla debate

pages.title: Money is not a secret
pages.body: After decades of inflation, prices are everyone's favorite topic. **¿Cuánto pagaste?** (how much did you pay?) is a normal question about your phone, your rent, your shoes. Friends may even ask **¿cuánto ganás?** (how much do you earn?). It's not rude here, it's comparing notes to survive. Same with **¿cuánto te salió?** (what did it cost you?).

pages.title: Estás más gordito
pages.body: Your aunt sees you after the holidays and says **estás más gordito** (you've put on a little weight). Nobody here thinks that's an insult. It's said with affection, like "you're looking well fed". Many couples call each other **gordo** or **gorda** as a pet name, whatever their size. Younger people are more careful with body comments, though.

pages.scenario: Your friend's grandmother pinches your cheek and says: "¡Ay, estás más gordito!"
pages.prompt: What's the best reaction?
options: Look offended and change the subject
Laugh and say something like "¡Es que como bien!"
Explain that you've been going to the gym
pages.explain: It's a warm comment, not a diet review. Laugh it off. She'll probably serve you a second plate anyway.

pages.statement: When an Argentine partner calls you "gorda", they're usually commenting on your weight.
pages.explain: **Gordo/gorda** is one of the most common pet names in the country, like *honey*. **Flaco** (skinny) is also a common way to call a guy you don't know: "¡Flaco, se te cayó esto!"

pages.title: Viveza criolla
pages.body: **Viveza criolla** is the habit of getting ahead by being sharp: cutting the line, dodging a rule, finding the trick. In 1965 the sociologist **Julio Mafud** wrote a whole book on it, and people still argue about it at every sobremesa. Is it a national flaw, or just a stereotype?

pages.title: The two sides
pages.body: Critics say it wears down trust: if everyone expects the other guy to cheat, nobody plays fair, and rules stop working. Others push back: most Argentines are honest people tired of the label, and a lot of that sharpness is just **rebusque**, the art of getting by when the economy keeps collapsing. Both views are common, often in the same person.

pages.title: The flip side: la gauchada
pages.body: If viveza is the dark side, **la gauchada** is the bright one: a favor done for free, just because. Lending the neighbor your drill, driving a friend to the airport at 5 a.m., a stranger helping you push your car. **¿Me hacés una gauchada?** (can you do me a favor?) is one of the nicest questions in the language.

pages.scenario: Your coworker asks: "¿Me hacés una gauchada? Mañana necesito que me cubras una hora."
pages.prompt: What is she asking for?
options: A favor: to cover for her for an hour
To go out with her after work
pages.explain: A **gauchada** is a favor. The word comes from **gaucho**, the countryside horseman, famous for helping strangers on the road.

pages.prompt: Match the phrase to its meaning
pairs: You've put on a bit of weight (said kindly)

example.en: Honey, can you bring bread?
Hey man, do you have the time?

vocabulary.en: getting by, finding a way to make money

example.en: I get by doing whatever comes up.
Can you do me a favor?
Nice sneakers, how much were they?

classes.title: Christmas in summer
classes.summary: Cider, vitel toné and fireworks at midnight

pages.title: Santa in 35 degrees
pages.body: In Argentina Christmas falls in summer. It can be 35 °C, and Papá Noel is still in his wool coat. Families put up the **arbolito** (Christmas tree) on **8 December**, a public holiday. The big night is not the 25th: it's **Nochebuena**, the night of the 24th, with a long dinner, often outside, that ends well after midnight.

pages.title: The Christmas table
pages.body: The food is mostly cold, because of the heat. The star is **vitel toné**: thin slices of veal in a creamy tuna sauce, brought by immigrants from Piedmont, in Italy. Then **pan dulce** (a panettone-style sweet bread), **turrón** (nougat), **garrapiñada** (candied peanuts) and cider. Yes, there's often an asado too.

pages.prompt: Match the Christmas food to what it is

pages.title: Twelve o'clock
pages.body: At midnight on the 24th everyone stands up for the **brindis** (toast), with **sidra** or champagne, and says **¡Feliz Navidad!** The sky explodes with fireworks from every backyard and balcony. Then the presents: in most homes they're opened right then, at midnight, not on the morning of the 25th. The 25th is for leftovers and naps.
pages.fun_fact: Many families play **amigo invisible** (Secret Santa) so nobody has to buy twenty gifts.

pages.statement: Argentine kids usually open their Christmas presents on the morning of 25 December.
pages.explain: Most open them right after midnight on the 24th, with the fireworks going off. The morning of the 25th is very quiet.

pages.prompt: Nochebuena, in order
items: Pan dulce and turrón until late

pages.title: Año Nuevo and the paper rain
pages.body: New Year's Eve repeats the formula: dinner, a toast at midnight, fireworks. On the last working day of the year, office workers downtown used to throw paper out of the windows, covering the streets of the **microcentro**. The city has tried to discourage it for years, but some still do it. Then everyone heads for the beach, because January is holiday month.
pages.fun_fact: On 6 January, kids leave their shoes out with grass and water for the camels of the **Reyes Magos** (Three Kings).

pages.prompt: It's midnight on 24 December and everyone raises a glass. What do you say?
pages.translation: Merry Christmas!
pages.explain: On the 24th it's **Feliz Navidad**. A week later, at midnight on the 31st, it's **Feliz Año Nuevo**. Both come with a kiss for everyone at the table.

pages.scenario: You're invited to Nochebuena with your partner's family. It's 34 °C.
pages.prompt: What's most likely on the table?
options: Hot turkey with gravy and roast potatoes
Vitel toné, cold salads and pan dulce
Only sweets, dinner is on the 25th
pages.explain: Cold food rules in the heat. Vitel toné, **ensalada rusa** (potato salad) and pan dulce are the classics. Some families still roast something, heat or no heat.

example.en: We put up the tree on the 8th.

example.es: ¡Vamos al brindis, que son las doce!
example.en: Time for the toast, it's midnight!
Where are you spending the holidays?

classes.title: The calendar
classes.summary: Friends' Day, spring, Carnaval, long weekends and birthdays

pages.title: Día del Amigo
pages.body: On **20 July 1969** humans walked on the Moon, and an Argentine teacher and dentist, **Enrique Febbraro**, decided it should be a day of friendship for the whole world. He sent a thousand letters to a hundred countries. Today **20 de julio** is **Día del Amigo**: restaurants are packed and everyone messages everyone.
pages.fun_fact: In the 2000s so many texts were sent that the phone networks reportedly collapsed.

pages.statement: Día del Amigo on 20 July was an Argentine idea, inspired by the Moon landing.
pages.explain: Febbraro's idea: if humans could reach the Moon together, the world could celebrate friendship together. Uruguay and Brazil also celebrate it on 20 July.

pages.title: Spring and students
pages.body: **21 September** is a double party: the first day of spring and the **Día del Estudiante**. It honors **Sarmiento**, the president who pushed public schools, whose remains came back to Buenos Aires in September 1888. Students get the day off and fill the parks with picnics, guitars and music.

pages.title: Carnaval and long weekends
pages.body: **Carnaval** Monday and Tuesday are public holidays, with **murgas** (street bands in costumes, drums and dance) and foam sprays. The last dictatorship removed the holiday in 1976, and it only came back in 2011. Argentines also love **fines de semana largos** (long weekends): the government can add up to three **feriados puente**, bridge days that connect a holiday to the weekend.

pages.scenario: Your friend says: "El jueves es feriado y el viernes es puente. ¿Nos vamos a la costa?"
pages.prompt: What is she proposing?
options: A four-day trip to the beach
Working on Friday to cover the holiday
pages.explain: A **puente** turns a Thursday holiday into a four-day weekend. Argentines plan trips around them months in advance.

pages.title: Que los cumplas feliz
pages.body: The birthday song here goes **Que los cumplas feliz** (may you have a happy birthday), to the usual tune. Then the **tirón de orejas**: friends pull your ears, one tug for each year. And never wish someone **feliz cumple** before the day. It's bad luck. The story goes that even Pope Francis, from Buenos Aires, warned a crowd who greeted him early.

pages.scenario: Your friend's birthday is tomorrow. You won't see her, so you want to text her today.
pages.prompt: What should you do?
options: Text "feliz cumple" today, early is fine
Send a present with no message
pages.explain: Early birthday wishes are **yeta** (bad luck). Wait until the day. At midnight is ideal: the first message wins.

pages.prompt: Match the date to the celebration
pages.explain: Mother's Day in October, not May, surprises a lot of visitors. It goes back to a 1930s Catholic feast for Mary's motherhood.

pages.prompt: It's your friend's birthday. Everyone stands up to sing.
pages.text: Que los cumplas ___, que los cumplas feliz…
pages.translation: May you have a happy birthday…
pages.explain: The whole song is **que los cumplas feliz**, four times, with the name in the third line. Then the ears.

example.en: Happy birthday!

vocabulary.en: bridge day between a holiday and the weekend

example.en: What are you doing on the long weekend?

example.es: No me saludes antes, que es yeta.
example.en: Don't wish me early, it's bad luck.

sections.title: Buenos Aires
sections.summary: Barrios, bondis, cafés and the city that never goes to bed

classes.title: Porteños and everyone else
classes.summary: Capital, Provincia, el interior, and what they say about each other

pages.title: People of the port
pages.body: People from Buenos Aires are **porteños**, from **puerto** (port). For centuries the city was the country's gate to the world: ships, goods and millions of immigrants all came in through here. That's why porteños grew up looking at Europe across the water, and why the rest of the country sometimes says they forget there's a whole Argentina behind them.

pages.title: Capital is not Provincia
pages.body: Here's the tricky part. The city, **CABA** (Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires), has about 3 million people and 48 official **barrios**. It's *not* part of the **Provincia de Buenos Aires**, which wraps around it. The avenue **General Paz** and the **Riachuelo** river mark the border. Cross it and you're in the **conurbano**, the huge ring of suburbs where millions more live.
pages.fun_fact: The city only got to elect its own mayor, the **Jefe de Gobierno**, after the 1994 constitutional reform.

pages.scenario: A friend from Quilmes, just outside the city, says: "Mañana voy a Capital a hacer unos trámites."
pages.prompt: Where is she going?
options: Into the city of Buenos Aires
To La Plata, the provincial capital
pages.explain: People in the conurbano say **Capital** (or **Capi**) for the city itself. Funny detail: the capital of the *Provincia* is actually **La Plata**, not Buenos Aires.

pages.title: And then, el interior
pages.body: Porteños tend to call everywhere outside the metro area **el interior**. People from Córdoba, Mendoza or Salta don't always love that: it makes the whole country sound like a backyard. They have a famous comeback: **"Dios está en todas partes, pero atiende en Buenos Aires"**. God is everywhere, but he keeps office hours in Buenos Aires. It's a dig at how much money and power sit in the city.

pages.statement: "Dios está en todas partes, pero atiende en Buenos Aires" is a compliment about how great the city is.
pages.explain: It's a complaint. It means everything important gets decided in Buenos Aires, and the provinces have to go ask. The Buenos Aires–interior tension goes back to the 1800s fights over the port's customs money.

pages.title: The stereotypes, both ways
pages.body: The rest of the country says porteños are **agrandados** (full of themselves), talk too fast and think the world ends at the General Paz. Porteños joke that people in the provinces live slower, take the **siesta** seriously and never hurry. Both sides exaggerate, and both sides laugh. Just don't tell someone from Córdoba they sound "like a porteño".
pages.fun_fact: Abroad, anyone from the whole metro area often just says "soy de Buenos Aires". At home, the difference matters.

pages.prompt: Match the word to what it means
pairs: from the city of Buenos Aires
the city, as people from the suburbs call it
the ring of suburbs around the city
the rest of the country, porteño-style

pages.scenario: You're in Mendoza and a local asks where you've been. You say: "Estuve en Buenos Aires y ahora estoy conociendo el interior." He raises an eyebrow.
pages.prompt: What happened?
options: You sounded like a porteño who thinks everything else is "the inside"
pages.explain: Nothing terrible, but **el interior** is the porteño view of the map. Outside Buenos Aires, people prefer you just name the province: "estoy recorriendo Mendoza".

pages.prompt: Tell someone you're from the city itself
pages.translation: I'm from Buenos Aires, I was born in Palermo.
pages.explain: **Porteño** / **porteña**. The **puerto** is the port itself, not the people.

example.en: Are you from Buenos Aires? I can tell by your accent.

vocabulary.en: the city of Buenos Aires (said from the suburbs)

example.es: Laburo en Capital pero vivo en Lanús.
example.en: I work in the city but I live in Lanús.

classes.title: A city of barrios
classes.summary: From Caminito to Barrio Chino, each barrio has its own personality

pages.title: La Boca and Caminito
pages.body: **La Boca** sits where the Riachuelo meets the river, and it was filled with Genoese sailors and dockworkers. Its houses were built of wood and **chapa** (corrugated metal). The story goes they were painted with leftover paint from the shipyards. In 1959 the painter **Benito Quinquela Martín** pushed to turn an old alley into **Caminito**, named after a famous tango by Juan de Dios Filiberto.

pages.statement: Caminito got its name from a tango.
pages.explain: The tango "Caminito" (1926) had music by **Juan de Dios Filiberto**, from La Boca. In 1959 the city officially named the street after it, at Quinquela Martín's request.

pages.title: San Telmo on Sundays
pages.body: **San Telmo** is the old colonial south: cobblestones, balconies, antique shops. Every Sunday, **Plaza Dorrego** and calle **Defensa** fill up with the **Feria de San Telmo**, a street market started in 1970 with just 30 stalls. Today you'll find old soda siphons, vinyl, silverware, tango dancers on the corner and a lot of people **mirando nomás** (just looking).

pages.title: Palermo, the barrio that keeps splitting
pages.body: **Palermo** is the biggest barrio, so people keep inventing sub-barrios. **Palermo Soho** is bars, design shops and brunch. **Palermo Hollywood** got its name in the 2000s, when TV channels and production companies moved in. Real estate agents have added more (Palermo Chico, Palermo Botánico...). Joke among porteños: soon everything will be "Palermo something".

pages.prompt: Suggest a Sunday plan
pages.text: ¿Vamos el domingo a la ___ de San Telmo?
pages.translation: Shall we go to the San Telmo market on Sunday?
pages.explain: A **feria** is a street market. There are ferias all over the city, but San Telmo's is the classic one.

pages.title: Recoleta: a city of the dead
pages.body: The **Cementerio de la Recoleta** opened in 1822 as the city's first public cemetery. It's a maze of marble **bóvedas** (family vaults), with presidents, writers and lots of cats. **Evita** rests in the Duarte family vault. The most told legend is **Rufina Cambaceres**, a 19-year-old said to have been buried alive in 1902. Historians doubt it, but everyone stops at her tomb.

pages.title: Once, Villa Crespo, Barracas, Barrio Chino
pages.body: **Once** isn't an official barrio: it's the busy area around Once station, in Balvanera, full of wholesale shops and long home to much of the Jewish community, like neighboring **Villa Crespo**. In **Barracas**, artist Marino Santa María covered **Pasaje Lanín** in paint and mosaics. And in **Belgrano**, calle Arribeños became **Barrio Chino**, started by Taiwanese immigrants in the 1980s.

pages.scenario: A friend says: "Voy a Once a comprar tela, es mucho más barato." You check the official map of the 48 barrios.
pages.prompt: What do you find?
options: There's no barrio called Once; it's part of Balvanera
pages.explain: Everyone says **Once**, but it's a nickname from the **Once de Septiembre** train station. The official barrio is **Balvanera**. Same thing happens with **Barrio Chino**, which sits inside Belgrano.

pages.prompt: Match the barrio to what it's known for

example.en: There's a market in the square on Sundays.

classes.title: Bondi, subte, tacho
classes.summary: How to get around without getting lost (or run over)

pages.title: A porteño invention
pages.body: On **24 September 1928**, taxi drivers short on customers met at a bar on Rivadavia and Lacarra and had an idea: take several passengers at once, each paying a small fare, along a fixed route. That was the first **taxi colectivo**. It grew into the **colectivo**, the city bus. 24 September is still celebrated as the **Día del Colectivo**.

pages.title: Why "bondi"?
pages.body: Nobody says "autobús". It's **colectivo**, or even more often, **bondi**. The word comes from Brazil, where trams were called **bonde**, from the English *bond*, the tickets the British tram companies sold. In Buenos Aires **bondi** first meant the tram. When the trams disappeared in the 1960s, the name jumped to the bus.

pages.statement: "Bondi" is a word that originally meant tram, not bus.
pages.explain: It came via Brazilian Portuguese **bonde** (tram). Buenos Aires ripped out its trams, but kept the word.

pages.title: Wave, tell, tap
pages.body: Colectivos only stop if you ask. At the **parada** (stop), stick your arm out when yours comes, or it'll fly right past. Fares go by distance, so you tell the **chofer** where you're going, then tap your **SUBE** card (since 2025 many lines also take a contactless bank card). To get off, press the **timbre** (bell) before your stop and use the back door. Porteños also **hacen la cola**: they line up at the stop.

pages.prompt: Take a colectivo, step by step
items: Wait at the parada for your line
Stick your arm out when it comes
Tell the chofer where you're going
Press the timbre before your stop
pages.explain: Skip the arm and it won't stop. Skip the timbre and you'll ride to the next one.

pages.scenario: You get to the stop. Six people are standing in a neat line along the wall. The bus pulls up right in front of you.
pages.prompt: What do you do?
options: Get on, you're closest to the door
Go to the end of the line
Ask the driver to wait while you decide
pages.explain: The **cola** at the parada is sacred. Cut it and you'll get a loud **"¡Hay cola, eh!"** from the whole line.

pages.title: The subte and the tachos
pages.body: The **subte** (metro) opened on **1 December 1913**, the first in Latin America and the southern hemisphere, and older than Madrid's. Today it has lines A, B, C, D, E and H, each with its own color. Taxis are painted **black and yellow**, a rule since 1966. In slang, a taxi is a **tacho**.
pages.fun_fact: The same SUBE card works on colectivos, subte and trains.

pages.prompt: Match the word to the ride
You're on the bus and want to check you're going the right way. You ask the chofer:
pages.translation: Will you drop me at Plaza Italia? (Does this go to Plaza Italia?)
pages.explain: **¿Me deja en...?** is the classic question to the chofer. Most will answer quickly, and some will even tell you when it's your stop.

example.es: Me tomo el bondi y llego en veinte.
example.en: I'll catch the bus and be there in twenty.

classes.title: Obelisco, Colón and a pink house
classes.summary: The landmarks, and the stories porteños tell about them

pages.title: The Obelisco: built in a month, almost torn down
pages.body: The **Obelisco** went up in **1936**, for the 400th anniversary of the city's first founding. Workers built it in just **31 days**; it's 67.5 m tall. Lots of porteños hated it. In **1939** the city council actually voted to demolish it, and the mayor vetoed the decision. Today it's where the whole city goes to celebrate, or protest.

pages.title: The widest avenue in the world?
pages.body: The Obelisco stands on **Avenida 9 de Julio**. Porteños will proudly tell you it's **la avenida más ancha del mundo**: about **140 meters** if you count the side streets, with up to seven lanes each way. Brazilians like to argue that Brasília's **Eixo Monumental** is wider, but that's two roads with a giant lawn in between: Guinness lists it for the widest *median strip*, and 9 de Julio as the widest avenue.
pages.fun_fact: Crossing 9 de Julio on foot usually takes more than one green light.

pages.statement: Guinness lists Brasília's Eixo Monumental as the widest avenue in the world.
pages.explain: Guinness lists the Eixo Monumental for its huge **median strip**, the lawn between its two roads. The widest-avenue title goes to 9 de Julio, which porteños will happily remind you of.

pages.title: Why is the Casa Rosada pink?
pages.body: The president's office on **Plaza de Mayo** is the **Casa Rosada**. The popular story: in the 1860s–70s, President **Sarmiento** had it painted pink to mix the **red** of the federales with the **white** of the unitarios, the two old rival factions. Many historians give a messier answer: back then walls were painted with lime mixed with **cow's blood**, which helped against the damp.

pages.prompt: What's the practical explanation many historians give for the pink?
options: Lime paint mixed with cow's blood
The sunset reflected off the river
pages.explain: Lime plus blood was a common mix, and it held up against Buenos Aires' famous **humedad**. The red-plus-white story is nicer, so that's the one you'll hear on tours.

pages.title: Teatro Colón
pages.body: The **Teatro Colón** opened on **25 May 1908** with Verdi's *Aida*. Singers and conductors rank its horseshoe-shaped hall among the best in the world for opera acoustics. You don't need a gala ticket to see it: there are daily guided tours, and cheap seats way up high in the **paraíso**, the top gallery.

pages.title: Café Tortoni and the cafés notables
pages.body: The **Café Tortoni**, on Avenida de Mayo, opened in **1858**: it's the oldest café in the city. Borges, Gardel and Lorca all passed through. It's one of the **bares notables**, historic cafés the city protects. Porteño café rule: order a **cortado**, sit for two hours, read, argue. Nobody will rush you, and the **mozo** won't bring the check until you ask.

pages.scenario: You've been at a café for an hour and a half with one cortado. You're ready to leave, but the mozo hasn't brought the check.
pages.prompt: What's going on?
options: He's annoyed you stayed so long
In Buenos Aires you ask for the check; bringing it unasked is almost rude
You're expected to pay at the counter
pages.explain: Bringing the check unasked feels like kicking you out. Catch the mozo's eye and say **"¿Me traés la cuenta?"**.

pages.prompt: Match the landmark to its story
pairs: pink, maybe thanks to cow's blood
oldest café in the city, since 1858

pages.prompt: Order at a café like a local
pages.text: Un ___ y dos medialunas, por favor.
pages.translation: A cortado and two medialunas, please.
pages.explain: A **cortado** is espresso "cut" with a bit of milk. With **medialunas** it's the classic café order.

vocabulary.en: espresso with a splash of milk

example.en: Excuse me! Can you bring me the check?

example.es: No es el calor, es la humedad.
example.en: It's not the heat, it's the humidity.

vocabulary.note: The most repeated sentence of every porteño summer.

vocabulary.en: top gallery of a theater (cheapest seats)

classes.title: Life in the ciudad de la furia
classes.summary: Therapists, dog walkers, bookshops, late nights, and street smarts

pages.title: Everyone has a psicólogo
pages.body: Argentina has one of the highest numbers of psychologists per person in the world: a 2016 WHO report counted about **222 per 100,000** people, the highest figure it recorded. A big share work in Buenos Aires. Going to therapy isn't a secret here. **"Lo hablo con mi psicóloga"** is a normal thing to say at a dinner.

pages.statement: In Buenos Aires, people usually keep quiet about going to therapy.
pages.explain: Quite the opposite. **Hacer terapia** is so normal that people quote their therapist to friends. Psychoanalysis especially has deep roots here.

pages.title: The paseaperros
pages.body: Walk around Palermo or Recoleta and you'll see a **paseaperros** (dog walker) being dragged along by a pack of dogs, all on leashes, all different sizes. City rules actually cap it at **8 dogs** at once, and anyone walking more than 3 is supposed to be registered. Big packs still show up, and they get right of way on the sidewalk.

pages.title: Books and theater
pages.body: **El Ateneo Grand Splendid**, on Santa Fe avenue, was a 1919 theater. Since 2000 it's a bookshop, with books in the old boxes and a café on the stage; National Geographic called it the most beautiful bookshop in the world. And avenida **Corrientes** is the city's Broadway: theaters, bookshops open late, pizza at midnight. People call it **la calle que nunca duerme**.

pages.scenario: A porteño friend invites you to dinner "temprano, tipo nueve y media".
pages.prompt: What should you expect?
options: They made a mistake, dinner is at 7
That's genuinely early for a porteño dinner
pages.explain: Dinner at 9:30 or 10 pm is normal, and on weekends people go out even later. Show up at 8 and you'll catch them in the shower.

pages.title: The ciudad de la furia
pages.body: In 1988 Soda Stereo released **"En la ciudad de la furia"**, and the name stuck to Buenos Aires: fast, loud, horns honking, everyone in a hurry. Most of it is noise, not danger. But be smart with your phone: the famous thief is the **motochorro**, who grabs a phone from the back of a motorbike. Keep it off café tables by the street.

pages.scenario: You're at a café table on the sidewalk. You put your phone next to your cup. Your porteño friend moves it into your bag.
pages.prompt: Why?
options: Phones on the table are rude
A phone at the edge of a street table is an easy grab
pages.explain: Nobody's paranoid, just **atento** (alert). Phone in your pocket, backpack in front on a crowded colectivo, and you'll be fine. You'll hear **"¡Ojo con el celu!"** a lot.

pages.prompt: Warn a friend who's holding his phone at the curb
pages.text: ___ con el celu, que pasan motochorros.
pages.translation: Careful with your phone, there are bike thieves around.
pages.explain: **¡Ojo!** literally means "eye!": watch out. It's the most useful warning word in the city.

pages.prompt: Match the porteño to what they do
pairs: listens to your problems, for a fee

example.en: I've been in therapy for five years.

example.es: ¡Ojo con la mochila en el subte!
example.en: Watch your backpack on the metro!

sections.title: Las provincias
sections.summary: Argentina beyond Buenos Aires, from the salt flats to the end of the world

classes.title: Buenos Aires is not Argentina
classes.summary: A huge country, 24 districts and one big word: el interior

pages.title: Bigger than you think
pages.body: Argentina is the **eighth-largest country** in the world: about 2.8 million km², roughly five times France. From **La Quiaca**, on the Bolivian border, to **Ushuaia**, at the bottom of the map, you've got deserts at 4,000 m, jungle, vineyards, the pampa and glaciers. The legendary **Ruta 40** runs along the Andes for about 5,000 km. Pack a jacket *and* sunscreen.

pages.title: 23 plus one
pages.body: The country has **23 provincias** plus the **Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires** (**CABA**), the capital, which is *not* a province. Confusing part: there's also a **provincia de Buenos Aires**, the biggest one, surrounding the city. Its capital isn't Buenos Aires at all, it's **La Plata**. The smallest province is **Tucumán**; the youngest is **Tierra del Fuego**, which only became a province in 1990.

pages.statement: The city of Buenos Aires is the capital of the province of Buenos Aires.
pages.explain: The city is its own district, CABA. The province's capital is **La Plata**, about an hour south. Porteños mix this up too, don't worry.

pages.title: El interior
pages.body: In Buenos Aires, anything outside the city and its suburbs is **el interior**. "Se fue a vivir al interior" can mean Córdoba or a village of 300 people. The metro area (**AMBA**) holds about **a third** of all Argentines, so the capital tends to think it *is* the country. People from the provinces have noticed, and they have opinions.
pages.fun_fact: Someone from the provinces is a **provinciano**. Someone from the city is a **porteño**, from the port.

pages.scenario: You meet a girl in Palermo. She tells you she's from Salta and just moved to Buenos Aires for university.
pages.prompt: Which reply goes down best?
pages.explain: Asking what she misses (**¿qué extrañás?**) gets you twenty minutes about empanadas, family and the mountains. Calling her porteña is a quick way to get corrected: provincial identity runs deep.

pages.title: The map in five pieces
pages.body: Argentines usually split the country into regions: the **Noroeste** (NOA: Salta, Jujuy, Tucumán…), the **Noreste** and **Litoral** (Misiones, Corrientes, Santa Fe…), **Cuyo** (Mendoza, San Juan, San Luis), the **Centro** or pampa (Buenos Aires, Córdoba, La Pampa) and **Patagonia** down south. Each has its own accent, its own food and its own jokes about the others.

pages.prompt: Match the place to what you call someone from there
pages.explain: There's no single rule: -eño, -ino, -és, -ano. You just learn them. Getting it right earns you instant points.

pages.prompt: Put these provinces in order, from north to south
pages.explain: Jujuy touches Bolivia; Tierra del Fuego is an island across the Strait of Magellan. In between, well over 4,000 km of road.

pages.prompt: A porteño friend tells you his sister moved away from Buenos Aires.
pages.text: Mi hermana se fue a vivir al ___.
pages.translation: My sister moved out to the provinces.
pages.explain: **Al interior** means anywhere in the provinces. **Al exterior** would mean abroad. **Al campo** is the countryside, a farm, not a city like Rosario.

example.en: What province are you from?

vocabulary.note: Said mostly from Buenos Aires. Some provincianos find it a bit porteño-centric.

vocabulary.en: someone from the city of Buenos Aires

example.en: Tomorrow I'm going to Buenos Aires city.
I really miss my mum.
We're taking Route 40.

classes.title: The Noroeste: Andes, coca and Pachamama
classes.summary: Salta, Jujuy and the most Andean corner of the country

pages.title: Another Argentina
pages.body: Fly two hours north of Buenos Aires and you land in the Andes. **Salta** (nicknamed **Salta la linda**, Salta the pretty) and **Jujuy** feel closer to Bolivia and Peru than to Palermo: adobe villages, llamas, **ponchos**, quinoa, and Quechua words in everyday Spanish. The **Quebrada de Humahuaca**, a long valley in Jujuy, has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2003.

pages.title: The hill of seven colors
pages.body: In the little town of **Purmamarca**, the **Cerro de los Siete Colores** looks hand-painted: stripes of red, purple, ochre and green, from different minerals laid down over millions of years. Further up, at around **3,450 m**, the **Salinas Grandes** are a blinding white salt flat, over 200 km² of it. Everyone takes the same fake-perspective photo. You will too.

pages.statement: The Cerro de los Siete Colores gets its stripes from paint added for tourists.
pages.explain: It's all geology: layers of different minerals and sediments. The paint-brush look is completely natural.

pages.title: Coquear
pages.body: In the northwest, lots of people **coquean**: they tuck coca leaves into their cheek and keep a wad, the **acullico**, there for hours. It fights altitude, cold and tiredness. It's no scandal: since 1989, national law says chewing coca leaves in their natural state is **not** drug use. A few leaves in your cheek are a world away from cocaine, which is very much illegal.
pages.fun_fact: The odd bit: the leaves are legal to chew, but importing them isn't. Most come across the Bolivian border anyway.

pages.scenario: On a bus to Humahuaca, the man next to you has a bulging cheek and offers you some leaves from a little bag.
pages.prompt: What's going on?
options: He's coqueando and offering to share
pages.explain: Coca leaf is shared like mate up there. Taking a few helps with the altitude. You can also just say **no, gracias**: nobody will be offended.

pages.title: Feeding the Earth
pages.body: Every **1 de agosto** the Andes celebrate the **Pachamama**, Mother Earth. Families dig a hole, the **boca**, and "feed" it with food, coca, chicha and wine, to thank her and ask for a good year. The ritual is called the **corpachada**, a word of Quechua origin. Meanwhile, all over Argentina, people drink **caña con ruda** that morning to keep winter's bad luck away.

pages.statement: On August 1st, many Argentines, even in Buenos Aires, drink a shot of caña con ruda.
pages.explain: It's cane liquor steeped with rue, drunk on an empty stomach, in one, three or seven sips. The tradition is Guaraní in origin but has spread everywhere.

pages.title: Zambas and carnavalito
pages.body: Salta is the home turf of the **zamba**, a slow, elegant folk dance where couples circle each other waving white **pañuelos** (handkerchiefs). Jujuy dances the **carnavalito**, in a line, to flutes and charangos. And Jujuy's **carnaval** starts with the **desentierro del diablo**: a cloth devil gets dug up from a pile of stones, and the whole town parties until he's buried again.
pages.fun_fact: Dicen que the red poncho with black stripes of Salta mourns General Güemes, the local independence hero.

pages.prompt: Match the word to what it is
pairs: wad of coca leaves in the cheek

pages.prompt: Your friend in Salta invites you to the Pachamama celebration.
pages.text: El primero de agosto le damos de ___ a la Pachamama.
pages.translation: On August 1st we feed the Pachamama.
pages.explain: **Darle de comer** means to feed. That's literally the idea of the corpachada.

example.es: Coqueá un poco, que ayuda con la altura.
example.en: Chew some coca, it helps with the altitude.

vocabulary.en: wad of coca leaves held in the cheek
vocabulary.note: Northwest word. In Buenos Aires few people know it.

vocabulary.en: cane liquor with rue, drunk on August 1st

example.en: The altitude got to me.

classes.title: Cuyo: wine, water and the siesta
classes.summary: Mendoza, Malbec and the highest mountain outside Asia

pages.title: An oasis in the desert
pages.body: **Cuyo** (Mendoza, San Juan, San Luis) is dry: the name is usually said to mean "land of sands". Mendoza lives on snowmelt from the Andes, channelled through **acequias**, open ditches along every street that water the trees. The system goes back to the **Huarpe** people, before the Spanish. Walk around at night and mind your step: falling into one is a rite of passage.

pages.title: Malbec country
pages.body: Mendoza produces most of Argentina's wine, and around **85% of its Malbec**. The grape came from France in the 1800s and found its real home here, in sun, altitude and dry air. Today it's the country's flagship wine, with its own day: **17 de abril**, Malbec World Day. A **bodega** is a winery, and visiting them by bike is a local classic.

pages.statement: Malbec was originally a French grape.
pages.explain: It comes from southwest France. It flopped there after frost and disease, and boomed in Mendoza. Argentines are not modest about this.

pages.title: La Vendimia
pages.body: Every year the grape harvest ends with the **Fiesta Nacional de la Vendimia**, official since **1936**. It builds up from January and peaks in early March, with parades, a giant open-air show in a stone amphitheater in the foothills, and the crowning of the **Reina de la Vendimia**, picked from queens sent by each of Mendoza's departments. It's Mendoza's biggest night, by far.

pages.title: El Aconcagua
pages.body: Right behind Mendoza stands the **Aconcagua**, at about **6,961 m** the highest mountain outside Asia, and the roof of the Americas. Thousands try to summit it each season; plenty turn back because of altitude and wind. You don't need to climb it: from the road to Chile you can see its snowy face from the Horcones lagoon.

pages.prompt: What makes the Aconcagua special?
options: It's the highest active volcano in the world
It's the highest mountain outside Asia
It's on the border with Bolivia
It's the only mountain in Argentina with snow
pages.explain: Almost 7,000 m, the highest point of both the western and southern hemispheres. It's entirely inside Argentina, near the Chilean border.

pages.title: La siesta is real
pages.body: In Buenos Aires the siesta is a weekend luxury. In Cuyo and much of the interior it's a schedule: lots of shops close in the early afternoon and reopen around five, and the streets go silent in the summer heat. Try calling someone at 3 p.m. and you'll get a sleepy voice, or no answer. People then stay up late when it cools down.

pages.scenario: It's 3 p.m. on a hot January weekday in San Juan. You need to buy a charger and the shop is shut.
pages.prompt: What's the most likely explanation?
options: It's closed for the siesta and will reopen later
pages.explain: Come back around five or six. The **horario cortado** (split opening hours) is normal in many provinces.

pages.prompt: A mendocino invites you out for the afternoon.
pages.translation: Shall we tour the wineries by bike?
pages.explain: **Bodega** is a winery (in other contexts, a storeroom). Pedal slowly: the tasting is at every stop.

pages.statement: The acequias in Mendoza's streets are just decorative fountains.
pages.explain: They're real irrigation channels. Without them, the city's trees, and the whole oasis, would die.

example.es: Mañana vamos a una bodega en Luján de Cuyo.
example.en: Tomorrow we're going to a winery in Luján de Cuyo.

vocabulary.en: to take a nap after lunch

example.es: No me llames a las tres, que duermo la siesta.
example.en: Don't call me at three, I'm napping.

vocabulary.en: split opening hours (closed in the afternoon)

example.en: Shall we order a red?

classes.title: Córdoba: fernet, cuarteto and the tonada
classes.summary: The province that talks slower, parties harder and jokes about everything

pages.title: La tonada
pages.body: You'll hear a cordobés before you see one. The **tonada** (or **cantito**) stretches the syllable *before* the stressed one: **"capiiital"**, **"cordoobés"**, with a little sing-song on top. Some linguists think it's a trace of the **Comechingón** languages spoken there before Spanish. Porteños love imitating it. Cordobeses love telling them they do it badly.

pages.title: La Docta
pages.body: Córdoba's nickname is **La Docta**, "the learned one". Its university, founded by the Jesuits in **1613**, is the oldest in the country, and for over two centuries it was the only one. Today the city is full of students from all over Argentina. The old Jesuit block downtown, the **Manzana Jesuítica**, is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

pages.statement: Córdoba is called "La Docta" because of its old university.
pages.explain: **Docta** means learned. The Universidad Nacional de Córdoba dates back to 1613, and for a long time it was the only university in the country.

pages.title: Fernet con coca
pages.body: **Fernet** is a bitter Italian herbal liqueur. Argentina drinks most of the world's supply, and Córdoba, with about 8% of the population, drinks around **a third** of the country's. Mixed with Coca-Cola, lots of ice, and a proper foam on top, it's the drink of every party. Some cordobeses pour it into a cut-off plastic bottle: the classic **fernet en bidón**.
pages.fun_fact: Argentines also call it a **fernando**. Nobody knows who Fernando was.

pages.scenario: At a party in Córdoba someone hands you a big glass of something dark and fizzy with a thick foam.
pages.prompt: What is it almost certainly?
pages.explain: **Fernet con coca**, the unofficial provincial drink. It's bitter the first time and addictive by the third. Pace yourself: fernet is strong stuff, the Coke just hides it.

pages.title: Cuarteto
pages.body: Córdoba's party music is **cuarteto**, born in **1943** with the **Cuarteto Leo**: Italian tarantella and pasodoble played for working-class dance halls, with a bouncy piano beat locals call **tunga-tunga**. Its king is **Carlos "La Mona" Jiménez**, on stage for more than fifty years. **Rodrigo**, "el Potro", made it national in the 90s, before dying in a car crash in 2000, aged 27.
pages.fun_fact: In December 2025 UNESCO added cuarteto to its list of intangible heritage of humanity.

pages.title: Culiado
pages.body: Cordobeses are famous for their humor: fast, cheeky, and full of **jodas** (teasing). Their signature word is **culiado** (said **culiao**). It's vulgar in origin, and still an insult if you say it angrily, but between friends it's closer to "mate" or "dude": "¿Qué hacés, culiao?" The story goes that even Paul McCartney greeted a Córdoba crowd with it.

pages.scenario: You've just met a group of cordobeses. One of them says to another, laughing: "¡Qué hacés, culiao!"
pages.prompt: Should you greet them the same way?
options: Yes, it's just a local hello
Better wait until you're friends, it's still rude with strangers
Never, it's the worst insult in Argentina
pages.explain: Between friends it's affection. From a gringo they just met, it can land badly. Tone and trust are everything. Wait until they call *you* culiao.

pages.prompt: Match the Córdoba icon to what it is
Your cordobés friend is organizing drinks.
pages.text: Traé hielo, que hacemos un ___ con coca.
pages.translation: Bring ice, we're making fernet and coke.
pages.explain: Fernet without ice is a crime in Córdoba. Somebody always forgets the ice anyway.

example.es: Se le nota la tonada cordobesa.
example.en: You can hear his Córdoba accent.

vocabulary.note: Vulgar origin. Use only with friends, and only if they use it first.

vocabulary.en: teasing, a joke; also a party

example.es: Era una joda, no te enojes.
example.en: It was a joke, don't get mad.
I love the Córdoba sing-song.

classes.title: The Litoral: rivers, falls and chamamé
classes.summary: Iguazú, Guaraní, Rosario and a very loud yell

pages.title: A coast with no sea
pages.body: The **Litoral** (Santa Fe, Entre Ríos, Corrientes, Misiones…) means "coast", but none of it touches the ocean. The coasts are **river** banks: the huge **Paraná** and **Uruguay** rivers. Up in the **Noreste**, the air is humid, the soil is bright red (**tierra colorada**), and **siesta**, **tereré** and fishing are serious business.

pages.title: Iguazú
pages.body: On the border with Brazil, the **Cataratas del Iguazú** are around **275 waterfalls** along almost 3 km, about 80% of them on the Argentine side. The star is the **Garganta del Diablo** (Devil's Throat), about 80 m of thundering water. The story goes that when US First Lady **Eleanor Roosevelt** saw it, she sighed: **"Poor Niagara!"** Nobody has found proof she said it, but everyone repeats it.

pages.statement: Most of the Iguazú waterfalls are on the Argentine side.
pages.explain: About 80% of the falls are in Argentina. Brazilians like to point out that their side has the better panoramic view. Both are right.

pages.title: Guaraní is still here
pages.body: The northeast is Guaraní land, and you can hear it. In **Corrientes**, Guaraní has been an official language alongside Spanish since **2004**. Everyday speech is full of Guaraní words: **gurí** / **gurisa** (kid, boy / girl), **mitaí** (child), **che** (my, as in "che ru", my father), **ñandú** (rhea). Many correntinos pepper their Spanish with it.

pages.title: Chamamé and the sapucai
pages.body: The Litoral's music is **chamamé**: accordion, guitar and couples dancing tightly embraced. Every January, **Corrientes** hosts the **Fiesta Nacional del Chamamé**. At the best moment of a song, someone lets out a **sapucai**: a long, high, piercing yell of joy (or grief, or bravery). In 2020 UNESCO listed chamamé as intangible heritage of humanity.

pages.scenario: You're at a chamamé dance in Corrientes. Suddenly a man next to you throws his head back and lets out a long, piercing scream.
pages.prompt: What's happening?
options: It's a sapucai, he's feeling the music
pages.explain: The **sapucai** (from Guaraní) is how chamamé fans express emotion. Nobody will expect you to do one. But if you try, go loud.

pages.title: Rosario
pages.body: **Rosario**, in Santa Fe, is Argentina's third city and a river town through and through. It's where Belgrano first raised the flag, hence its giant **Monumento a la Bandera**. It's also the birthplace of **Lionel Messi** (1987) and **Ernesto "Che" Guevara** (1928), and of rock star **Fito Páez**. In Santa Fe, a draft beer is ordered as a **liso**, served in a straight glass.

pages.prompt: Match the place to what it's famous for
Grandma in Corrientes uses a Guaraní word for the neighbor's boy. Which one?
pages.translation: That kid is really cheeky.
pages.explain: **Gurí** (from Guaraní) is what the Litoral and Uruguay call a boy. A **ñandú** is a rhea, and a **sapucai** is a yell. In Buenos Aires you'd hear **pibe**.

pages.statement: Che Guevara got his nickname because he was born in Buenos Aires.
pages.explain: He was born in **Rosario**. Cubans called him "Che" because he said it all the time, the most Argentine word there is.

example.en: Have you been to the Iguazú Falls?

vocabulary.note: Guaraní origin. In Buenos Aires they say pibe / piba.

vocabulary.en: long cry of emotion in chamamé
accordion folk music of the Litoral

example.en: Two draft beers, please.

classes.title: Patagonia: ice, wind and Welsh tea
classes.summary: Glaciers, whales, chocolate and the end of the world

pages.title: Big and empty
pages.body: **Patagonia** (Neuquén, Río Negro, Chubut, Santa Cruz, Tierra del Fuego) covers more than a quarter of Argentina, but only about **1 in 20** Argentines live there. It's steppe, lakes, the Andes and a wind that never stops. Gusts of 100 km/h are nothing special. You'll spot the tourists: they're the ones chasing their hats.

pages.title: The Perito Moreno
pages.body: Near **El Calafate**, the **glaciar Perito Moreno** ends in a wall of ice about 70 m tall. Every few years it pushes across the lake, builds an ice bridge, and the bridge collapses on live TV. For decades it was famous for being stable while other glaciers shrank. Bad news: studies now show it has been retreating since around 2020.
pages.fun_fact: Legend says whoever eats a **calafate** berry will come back to Patagonia.

pages.statement: The Perito Moreno glacier is still famous for being one of the few glaciers not affected by warming.
pages.explain: That used to be true. Recent studies show it started retreating around 2020, and the loss is speeding up.

pages.title: Te galés
pages.body: On **28 July 1865**, the ship **Mimosa** dropped about 150 **Welsh** settlers in what's now **Puerto Madryn**. They wanted a place to keep their language and chapels. They founded towns in the Chubut valley, like **Gaiman**, where today you can have a **té galés**: pots of tea, scones, jams and the **torta negra**, a dense fruit cake built to last through winter.

pages.title: Bariloche and the viaje de egresados
pages.body: **Bariloche** looks like the Alps: lakes, wooden chalets, ski slopes and **chocolate** shops on every corner. It's also where Argentine teens go on their **viaje de egresados**, the end-of-high-school trip: more than 100,000 a year, with tour-company **coordinadores** trying to keep them alive and sober. Almost every adult has stories. Few will tell you all of them.

pages.scenario: Your Argentine coworker, 35, shows you a photo of a bunch of teens in matching jackets in the snow.
pages.prompt: What's the photo almost certainly from?
options: Their viaje de egresados to Bariloche
pages.explain: The group jacket, the snow, the embarrassing haircuts: classic **viaje de egresados**. Ask about it and enjoy the story (the censored version).

pages.title: Whales and the end of the world
pages.body: From about **June to December**, southern right whales come to **Península Valdés** to mate and give birth, sometimes a few meters from the shore. Way further south, **Ushuaia** calls itself **el fin del mundo**, the end of the world. Its little **Tren del Fin del Mundo** was once used to take prisoners from the old jail out to cut wood.

pages.title: Cordero al asador
pages.body: Patagonia's great feast is **cordero patagónico al asador**: a whole lamb opened flat on an iron cross, stuck in the ground leaning over the fire, and cooked slowly for hours. The sheep graze wild on the steppe, so the meat tastes different. It's the southern cousin of the asado, and the waiting, with wine and conversation, is part of the plan.

pages.prompt: Put these Patagonian places in order, from north to south
pages.explain: Bariloche is in Río Negro, Valdés in Chubut, El Calafate in Santa Cruz and Ushuaia on the island of Tierra del Fuego.

pages.prompt: Match the place to what you go there for
A friend asks how your trip to Ushuaia was.

classes.title: Mafalda and her gang
classes.summary: The six-year-old who worried about the whole world

pages.title: The girl who hated soup
pages.body: **Mafalda** is a little girl with a big bow and bigger questions: world peace, the Beatles, and why grown-ups run things so badly. She was drawn by **Quino** (Joaquín Salvador Lavado), a cartoonist from Mendoza. Her first strip came out on **29 September 1964**, and she ended in 1973. Her mortal enemy? **La sopa**. She hates soup more than war, almost.
pages.fun_fact: Quino died on 30 September 2020, one day after Mafalda turned 56.

pages.statement: Mafalda was first created for an ad campaign for home appliances.
pages.explain: Quino first sketched her in 1963 for an ad for **Mansfield** appliances (that's why her name starts with M). The campaign never ran, and a year later she got her own strip.

pages.title: The gang
pages.body: **Felipe**: dreamy, shy, allergic to homework. **Manolito**: son of a Spanish **almacenero** (corner-shop owner), obsessed with money. **Susanita**: dreams only of a husband and kids, and gossips nonstop. **Miguelito**: a little philosopher in his own head. **Libertad**: tiny, with big political ideas. Plus **Guille**, Mafalda's baby brother. Every Argentine knows someone who's a Susanita or a Manolito.

pages.prompt: Match the character to their thing
pairs: works at his dad's almacén, loves money
wants to get married and have kids
the tiny one with big ideas

pages.scenario: Your friend's kid pushes away the bowl at dinner and crosses her arms.
pages.prompt: What's the classic Argentine joke to make?
pages.explain: Mafalda vs. soup is *the* running gag. In the strips, soup stands for everything you're forced to swallow, and a lot of readers saw politics in that bowl.

pages.title: A statue on a bench
pages.body: Quino lived in **San Telmo**, at the corner of **Chile and Defensa**, and that's where Mafalda's home is in the strip. Since 2009 a statue of her sits on a bench right there, and there's always a line of people waiting to take a photo next to her. Susanita and Manolito got statues nearby later, because of course they'd want in.

pages.prompt: At Manolito's family shop. What's it called?
pages.text: Manolito atiende el ___ de su papá.
pages.translation: Manolito works at his dad's corner shop.
pages.explain: An **almacén** is the old-school neighborhood grocery store. A **kiosco** also exists, but it sells candy and cigarettes, not groceries.

pages.statement: Mafalda is only famous in Argentina.
pages.explain: She's been translated into dozens of languages and is huge in Spain, Italy and all of Latin America. Umberto Eco wrote a famous introduction to the Italian edition.

classes.title: Comics, cartoons and snow
classes.summary: Patoruzú, Clemente, El Eternauta and the first animated film ever

pages.title: Patoruzú, the rich cacique
pages.body: **Patoruzú** is a Tehuelche **cacique** (chief) from Patagonia, created by **Dante Quinterno** in 1928. He's strong, noble, owns an enormous ranch, and gets fleeced by his city-slicker godfather **Isidoro Cañones**, a lazy porteño playboy. For decades kids read his magazine. Today the drawing style feels old-fashioned, but everyone over 40 knows his name.

pages.title: Clemente and the papelitos
pages.body: **Clemente** is a striped bird with no wings, drawn by **Caloi** in *Clarín* from 1973. In the **1978 World Cup**, a famous radio commentator, **José María Muñoz**, asked fans not to throw **papelitos** (paper confetti) so the country wouldn't look messy. Clemente said the opposite: **"¡Tiren papelitos, muchachos!"** The stadiums ended up covered in paper. The bird won.

pages.scenario: Argentina walks onto the pitch at the 1978 World Cup. Clemente is watching.
pages.prompt: What does he want the fans to do?
pages.explain: **Tirar papelitos** is still a thing in Argentine stadiums. Clemente's campaign was playful, but under a dictatorship even a bird cheering for mess felt a little rebellious.

pages.title: El Eternauta: deadly snow
pages.body: In **1957** writer **Héctor Germán Oesterheld** and artist **Francisco Solano López** started **El Eternauta**: a toxic snow falls on Buenos Aires, and anyone it touches dies. Juan Salvo and his friends survive by working together. The hero isn't one man, it's the group. That idea, often summed up as **nadie se salva solo** (nobody saves themselves alone), became a motto.

pages.title: The author who disappeared
pages.body: Oesterheld was politically active with the **Montoneros**. In **1977** the military dictatorship kidnapped him, and he was never seen again. His **four daughters** also disappeared, along with their partners and two grandchildren born in captivity. That's why the Eternauta's silhouette shows up on murals and at human-rights marches. It's a comic, and it's also memory.

pages.statement: The 2025 Netflix series of El Eternauta starred Ricardo Darín as Juan Salvo.
pages.explain: Directed by **Bruno Stagnaro**, it came out on 30 April 2025 and was the most-watched show in many countries. Suddenly half of Buenos Aires was saying **"nadie se salva solo"** again.

pages.title: Before Disney: El Apóstol
pages.body: In **1917** the Italian-Argentine **Quirino Cristiani** released **El Apóstol**, the world's first animated feature film, 20 years before *Snow White*. It mocked President Yrigoyen, who flies up to Olympus and sets Buenos Aires on fire to clean up corruption. Sadly, the only copy burned in a studio fire in 1926, so today it is a lost film.

pages.prompt: Match the creator to the creation
The motto of El Eternauta
pages.translation: Nobody saves themselves alone.
pages.explain: People quote it about everything from politics to helping a neighbor move house. It's the group, not the superhero.
