classes.title: The writers
classes.summary: Borges, Cortázar, Sabato, Alfonsina and the turtle from Pehuajó

pages.title: Borges, no Nobel
pages.body: **Jorge Luis Borges** wrote short, dizzying stories about labyrinths, mirrors and infinite libraries. He went almost blind, and in 1955 became director of the **Biblioteca Nacional**, a man surrounded by books he couldn't read. He was nominated for the Nobel again and again and never got it. His conservative politics probably didn't help. Argentines still take that personally.
pages.fun_fact: He's said to have joked that not giving him the Nobel had become a Scandinavian tradition.

pages.statement: Borges won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
pages.explain: Never. He's one of the most famous writers never to win it, and Argentines bring it up like an old football robbery.

pages.title: Rayuela: read it how you like
pages.body: **Julio Cortázar** published **Rayuela** (*Hopscotch*) in 1963. You can read it straight through, or jump around chapters following a map he gives you at the start, like a hopscotch game. It's set between Paris and Buenos Aires, and it made him an idol for students. Fun detail: he was born in Brussels and kept a slight French-sounding "r" all his life.

pages.title: Sabato, the gloomy one
pages.body: **Ernesto Sabato** trained as a physicist and worked at the Curie lab in Paris, then quit science for novels. **El túnel** (1948) opens with a man confessing he killed the woman he loved. Dark stuff. Later he led the commission that wrote **Nunca Más**, the report on the dictatorship's crimes. Many Argentines read El túnel in high school.

pages.title: Alfonsina and María Elena
pages.body: **Alfonsina Storni** was a feminist poet in the 1920s; she died in the sea at Mar del Plata in 1938, and the song **Alfonsina y el mar** keeps her alive. **María Elena Walsh** wrote the songs every Argentine kid sings: **Manuelita**, the turtle from **Pehuajó** who went to Paris, and **El Reino del Revés**, where everything is upside down.

pages.scenario: At a birthday party, a room full of adults suddenly starts singing "Manuelita vivía en Pehuajó…" with the kids.
pages.prompt: Who are they singing?
pages.explain: Walsh's songs cross generations. Parents learned them as kids and now sing them to theirs, word for word.

pages.text: Leé ___, la podés leer en el orden que quieras.
pages.translation: Read Rayuela, you can read it in whatever order you want.
pages.explain: **Rayuela** is also the Argentine name of the hopscotch game kids draw in chalk on the sidewalk.

pages.statement: Manuelita, from María Elena Walsh's song, is a turtle.
pages.explain: A turtle from Pehuajó who travels to Paris to get herself fixed up, because she's getting old. Pehuajó even has a Manuelita statue.

classes.title: Inventions and Nobels
classes.summary: The birome, fingerprints, the bypass and five Nobel prizes

pages.title: The birome
pages.body: In Argentina a ballpoint pen is a **birome**. **László Bíró**, a Hungarian journalist, arrived in 1940 and patented the pen here in **1943** with his partner **Juan Jorge Meyne**. **Bi**-ró + **Me**-yne = **birome**. Its first big customer was the British air force, because it didn't leak at altitude. Argentina's **Día del Inventor**, 29 September, is his birthday.

pages.prompt: In class, you need a pen
pages.translation: Can you lend me a pen?
pages.explain: Hardly anyone in Argentina says *bolígrafo*. It's **birome** (or **lapicera**), a brand name turned into a word, like Kleenex.

pages.title: Fingerprints solve a murder
pages.body: In **1892**, in **Necochea**, two children were murdered. Their mother, **Francisca Rojas**, blamed a neighbor. But police inspector **Eduardo Álvarez**, trained in the new system of **Juan Vucetich**, a Croatian immigrant at the La Plata police, compared a bloody fingerprint on a door with hers. It matched, and she confessed. It was the first crime in the world solved with fingerprints, and Argentina was the first country to use them for identification.

pages.title: The colectivo
pages.body: On **24 September 1928**, broke Buenos Aires taxi drivers had an idea: share the cab, charge each passenger a fixed fare, follow a route. The **taxi colectivo** was born. Soon they stretched the cars to fit more seats. Today the **colectivo** (or **bondi**) is the city bus, and 24 September is the **Día del Colectivo**.

pages.title: Favaloro and the bypass
pages.body: **René Favaloro** was a country doctor in La Pampa for twelve years, then went to the Cleveland Clinic. There, in **1967**, he did one of the first coronary **bypass** operations with a leg vein, and the technique spread worldwide. Back home he built a famous heart foundation. In 2000, drowning in the foundation's debts, he took his own life. The country still mourns him.

pages.statement: The first crime solved with fingerprints happened in Argentina.
pages.explain: Necochea, 1892, thanks to **Vucetich**. The fingerprint system he built was copied all over the world. The police school in Buenos Aires province carries his name.

pages.title: Five Nobels
pages.body: **Saavedra Lamas** (Peace, 1936) helped end the Chaco War. **Houssay** (Medicine, 1947) studied hormones. **Leloir** (Chemistry, 1970) worked on how the body handles sugars. **Pérez Esquivel** (Peace, 1980) defended human rights under the dictatorship. **Milstein** (Medicine, 1984) co-discovered monoclonal antibodies, and the original method was never patented.
pages.fun_fact: Legend says Leloir invented salsa golf (mayo + ketchup) at a Mar del Plata golf club in the 1920s.

pages.scenario: You're in Palermo and need to get to San Telmo. Your friend says: "Tomate el bondi, te deja en la puerta."
pages.prompt: What should you take?
pages.explain: **Bondi** is slang for **colectivo**, the bus. Pay with your **SUBE** card and don't expect it to stop unless you raise your hand.

classes.title: Modern icons
classes.summary: A Pope from Flores, the Generación Dorada, Las Leonas and two Oscars

pages.title: Francisco, from Flores
pages.body: **Jorge Mario Bergoglio** was born in **Flores**, Buenos Aires, in 1936. As archbishop he rode the **subte** and the colectivo. In **2013** he became **Pope Francis**, the first from the Americas and the first Jesuit. He loved tango and was a paying member of **San Lorenzo**, card number 88235. He died on 21 April 2025.
pages.fun_fact: After his death, fans noticed the card: 88 was his age, and 2:35 a.m. (Argentine time) the hour he died.

pages.statement: Every Argentine loved Pope Francis without reservations.
pages.explain: Many adored him. Others criticized his conservative Church positions, or felt he meddled in Argentine politics, and some wished he'd visited as Pope (he never did). Mention him at a dinner and you'll hear both sides.

pages.title: Manu and the Generación Dorada
pages.body: **Manu Ginóbili**, from **Bahía Blanca**, won **four NBA titles** with the San Antonio Spurs and made the eurostep famous. He led the **Generación Dorada** (Golden Generation): in **Athens 2004** Argentina beat the USA in the semifinal and took **Olympic gold** in basketball. Nobody expected that from a football country. Manu entered the Hall of Fame in 2022.

pages.title: Las Leonas and Vilas
pages.body: The women's field hockey team became **Las Leonas** (the Lionesses) at **Sydney 2000**, when they first wore a lioness on their shirts and won silver. More Olympic medals followed, and **Lucha Aymar** was named world player of the year eight times. Before them, **Guillermo Vilas** won four Grand Slams and 46 matches in a row in 1977, and made tennis popular here.

pages.scenario: At an asado, someone says: "Vilas fue número uno, lo que pasa es que el ranking estaba mal."
pages.prompt: What are they talking about?
pages.explain: In 1977 Vilas won almost everything, but the ATP computer ranked him No. 2 behind Connors. Argentines still feel robbed, and a 2020 Netflix documentary retold the whole fight.

pages.title: Two Oscars and Darín
pages.body: Argentina has two Oscars for foreign-language film: **La historia oficial** (1986) and **El secreto de sus ojos** (2010), starring **Ricardo Darín**. **Argentina, 1985**, also with Darín, was nominated in 2023 and won the Golden Globe, but not the Oscar. Darín is the face of Argentine cinema: *Nueve reinas*, *Relatos salvajes*, and now El Eternauta.

pages.statement: "Argentina, 1985" won the Oscar for best international film.
pages.explain: It was nominated and won the Golden Globe, but the Oscar went to a German film. The two Argentine Oscars are **La historia oficial** and **El secreto de sus ojos**.

pages.explain: **Capo** = boss, legend, someone brilliant. **Chanta** is a con man, and **boludo**… you know that one from the puteadas section.

sections.title: Historia: el nacimiento de un país
sections.summary: From the first peoples to the tango: how Argentina came to be, up to 1930

classes.title: Before Buenos Aires
classes.summary: The first peoples, and a city that had to be founded twice

pages.title: They were here first
pages.body: Long before any Spaniard showed up, this land was full of peoples: the **guaraníes** in the humid northeast, the **diaguitas** farming the valleys of the northwest, the **mapuches** in the south by the Andes, the **tehuelches** across Patagonia, and the **querandíes**, hunters of the pampa right where Buenos Aires stands today. Argentines call them **pueblos originarios** (original peoples).
pages.fun_fact: Iguazú comes from Guaraní and means roughly 'big water'. Fair enough.

pages.prompt: Match each people to where they lived
pages.explain: And the mapuches lived on both sides of the Andes, in the south. The map was never empty.

pages.title: Words that stayed
pages.body: You speak native languages every day here without noticing. From **quechua** (the Andean language of the Inca world): **cancha** (field, court), **choclo** (corn on the cob), **palta** (avocado) and even **mate** — the word first meant the gourd. From **guaraní**: **ñandú** (the local ostrich-like bird) and **yaguareté** (jaguar). So when you ask for a **tostado con palta**, say thanks to the Andes.

pages.scenario: At a parrilla, your friend asks if you want a **choclo** on the grill.
pages.prompt: What are they offering you?
pages.explain: **Choclo** is corn on the cob, a word from quechua. The avocado is **palta** — also quechua, and never 'aguacate' here.

pages.title: Buenos Aires, take one
pages.body: In **1536** the Spaniard **Pedro de Mendoza** founded a settlement on the Río de la Plata and named it after the Virgin of the good winds: **Santa María del Buen Ayre**. It went badly. Hunger, disease and fights with the **querandíes** crushed it, and by **1541** the survivors had abandoned it. Many sailed up the river to Asunción, in today's Paraguay.

pages.title: Take two
pages.body: In **1580**, **Juan de Garay** came down from Asunción and founded the city again — this time for good. That's why porteños talk about **la primera fundación** and **la segunda fundación**. For two centuries it stayed a small, muddy port, more famous for smuggling than for anything else. The real money was in the silver mines of **Potosí**, far up in today's Bolivia.
pages.fun_fact: **Porteño** literally means 'from the port' — that's what people from Buenos Aires are called.

pages.prompt: Put these in order
items: Pueblos originarios live across the land for thousands of years
Pedro de Mendoza founds Buenos Aires (1536)
The first Buenos Aires is abandoned (1541)
Juan de Garay founds it again (1580)

pages.statement: Buenos Aires has survived without interruption since its very first founding.
pages.explain: The first one (1536) was abandoned in 1541. The city that lasted is Garay's, from 1580.

pages.prompt: Your friend is from Buenos Aires. How do they describe themselves?
pages.translation: I'm from Buenos Aires.
pages.explain: **Porteño** — from the port. You'll hear it a hundred times a day.

example.en: Indigenous peoples lived here long before.
Are you from Buenos Aires?

classes.title: A viceroyalty and two British invasions
classes.summary: How a sleepy port became a capital, and threw out the British twice

pages.title: The Virreinato
pages.body: In **1776** the Spanish crown created the **Virreinato del Río de la Plata** (Viceroyalty of the River Plate), with Buenos Aires as its capital. It covered today's Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and Bolivia. Overnight the smuggling port became the boss, run by a **virrey** (viceroy) who answered to the king in Spain.

pages.prompt: Which of these countries was NOT part of the Virreinato del Río de la Plata?
pages.explain: Chile was a separate Spanish territory. The Virreinato covered Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and Bolivia.

pages.title: The Cabildo
pages.body: Every Spanish colonial city had a **cabildo**: the town council, and the building where it met. The one in Buenos Aires is still standing on **Plaza de Mayo**, white, with arches and a little tower. You can visit it — it's a museum now. Look closely: it's shorter than it used to be.
pages.fun_fact: It lost three arches in 1889 to open Avenida de Mayo, and three more in 1931. From eleven arches to five.

pages.title: The British are coming
pages.body: In **1806** a British force under **William Beresford** took Buenos Aires. The viceroy ran away to Córdoba — not his finest hour. Locals organized under **Santiago de Liniers** and kicked the British out that August: the **Reconquista**. In **1807** the British came back, bigger, with **John Whitelocke**. Porteños fought street by street, and won again: the **Defensa**.

pages.title: Hot water from the rooftops
pages.body: The story every Argentine kid learns: during the Defensa, neighbors threw boiling water and oil from the flat rooftops onto the British soldiers. Some of it is legend polished over time, but the street fighting was very real. And the lesson stuck: porteños had beaten an empire without Spain's help. Why keep obeying a viceroy?

pages.statement: When the British took Buenos Aires in 1806, the viceroy led the defense of the city.
pages.explain: Viceroy Sobremonte fled toward Córdoba with the treasury — and the British caught up with the treasure anyway. The locals, led by Liniers, did the fighting.

pages.scenario: Walking downtown, you pass a street called **Reconquista**. Later, in San Telmo, you walk down **Defensa**.
pages.prompt: What do those street names remember?
options: The victories against the British invasions
pages.explain: **Reconquista** (1806) and **Defensa** (1807): the two times porteños beat the British. Buenos Aires names its streets after its history.

pages.prompt: Put these in order
items: Juan de Garay founds Buenos Aires
Spain creates the Virreinato del Río de la Plata
The British take Buenos Aires and are expelled (Reconquista)
The British return and lose again (Defensa)

classes.title: May and July: the big dates
classes.summary: The Revolución de Mayo in 1810 and independence in 1816

pages.title: Spain in trouble
pages.body: In 1808 Napoleon invaded Spain and locked up its king. In **May 1810**, news arrived in Buenos Aires that Spain had almost completely fallen. Big question: if there's no king, who's in charge here? On **22 May** the city held a **cabildo abierto** — an open town meeting of leading neighbors — and voted to remove the viceroy.

pages.title: 25 de mayo de 1810
pages.body: On **25 May 1810** a new local government took over: the **Primera Junta** (First Board), led by **Cornelio Saavedra**. It still ruled in the name of the Spanish king, at least on paper, so it wasn't independence yet. But it was the first government chosen here, by people from here. This is the **Revolución de Mayo**, and it's why the main square is called **Plaza de Mayo**.
pages.fun_fact: The classic school drawing shows the crowd with umbrellas. Historians argue about it: umbrellas did exist in Buenos Aires, but they were an imported luxury, so that sea of umbrellas is probably exaggerated.

pages.scenario: It's the 25th of May and your friend offers you **locro** (a thick corn-and-meat stew) and **pastelitos** (fried pastries with quince).
pages.prompt: What are you celebrating?
options: The end of the British invasions
pages.explain: The 25th of May is the Revolución de Mayo. Locro and pastelitos are the patriotic menu — you'll see them again on the 9th of July.

pages.title: 9 de julio de 1816
pages.body: Six years of war later, delegates from the provinces met in a house in **San Miguel de Tucumán**, in the northwest. On **9 July 1816** the **Congreso de Tucumán** declared independence from Spain and from any foreign power. The country called itself the **Provincias Unidas en Sud América**. The house is now the **Casa Histórica**, a museum.

pages.statement: Argentina declared its independence in Buenos Aires, on the 25th of May.
pages.explain: Independence was declared in Tucumán, on 9 July 1816. The 25th of May (1810) is the revolution that started the process.

pages.prompt: Match the date to what happened
pairs: Cabildo abierto votes out the viceroy

pages.title: Walk the calendar
pages.body: Buenos Aires is a history book you can walk. **Avenida de Mayo** runs from the Casa Rosada to the Congress. **Avenida 9 de Julio**, the huge one with the Obelisco, is named after independence day. Both dates are **feriados** (public holidays), and almost every town in the country has a street called 25 de Mayo and another called 9 de Julio.

pages.text: Vamos a la avenida ___ de Julio, por favor.
pages.translation: Let's go to 9 de Julio Avenue, please.
pages.explain: **9 de Julio**: independence day, and the avenue with the Obelisco.

classes.title: San Martín, Belgrano and the flag
classes.summary: The general who crossed the Andes and the man who made the flag

pages.title: Belgrano's flag
pages.body: **Manuel Belgrano** was a lawyer and economist who ended up a general in the independence wars. On **27 February 1812**, by the Paraná river in **Rosario**, he raised a light blue and white flag for the first time. Buenos Aires wasn't thrilled — it was a bit too independent for 1812. Today Rosario has a giant **Monumento a la Bandera**.

pages.title: Why light blue and white?
pages.body: Kids learn the colors come from the sky and its clouds. Some historians argue they come from the colors of the Spanish royal house of Borbón instead. Nobody can prove either one. Before the flag came the **escarapela**, a light blue and white rosette people pin on their chest on patriotic days. The **sol de mayo** (May sun) in the middle came later.
pages.fun_fact: The 18th of May is Día de la Escarapela. Watch for the rosettes on kids' school uniforms.

pages.statement: Belgrano died a rich and famous man, and that's why his day is a holiday.
pages.explain: He died poor, in Buenos Aires, on 20 June 1820. That date is now Día de la Bandera (Flag Day), a holiday.

pages.title: San Martín crosses the Andes
pages.body: **José de San Martín**, born in **Yapeyú** (Corrientes) and trained as a soldier in Spain, had a bold plan: beat Spain in Peru by going through Chile. From **Mendoza** he built the **Ejército de los Andes** and in **1817** crossed the mountains — thousands of men, mules and horses over passes more than 4,000 meters high. He won at **Chacabuco** and helped free Chile, then Peru.

pages.scenario: You're in the Catedral Metropolitana, next to Plaza de Mayo, and see soldiers in old blue uniforms guarding a tomb.
pages.prompt: Whose tomb is it?
pages.explain: San Martín's mausoleum, guarded by the **Granaderos**, the cavalry regiment he founded. He died in France in 1850; his remains came home in 1880.

pages.prompt: Match the hero to the fact
pairs: raised the first flag in Rosario
crossed the Andes with an army
led the fight against the British in 1806

pages.prompt: Argentines call San Martín the father of the nation:
pages.translation: He's the Father of the Homeland.
pages.explain: **Padre de la Patria**. His day is 17 August, the anniversary of his death — another feriado.

pages.title: Independent... and now what?
pages.body: Winning independence was the easy part. Then came decades of civil wars between two camps. The **unitarios** wanted one strong central government run from Buenos Aires. The **federales** wanted the provinces to rule themselves. Behind it all: who keeps the money from the port of Buenos Aires? The provinces had a pretty good guess.

pairs: wanted a strong central government in Buenos Aires
wanted the provinces to govern themselves
a regional strongman with his own followers

pages.title: Rosas
pages.body: **Juan Manuel de Rosas**, a rich landowner and a federal, governed Buenos Aires from 1829 to 1832 and again from 1835 to **1852**, with near-total power. Red was the federal color, and wearing it was all but required. His enforcers, the **Mazorca**, terrorized opponents. He also defied the British and French fleets. He fell at the battle of **Caseros**, in 1852.

pages.title: Hero or tyrant?
pages.body: Argentines still argue about Rosas. For the liberals who came after him, like **Sarmiento**, he was a bloody tyrant. For the **revisionistas** (historians who rethought him in the 20th century), he defended national sovereignty against foreign powers. Today most academic historians step out of that duel and study how his rule worked, and why so many poor porteños and gauchos backed him. Don't bring it up at an asado unless you have time.
pages.fun_fact: The 20 November holiday, Día de la Soberanía Nacional, remembers a battle fought under Rosas against the Anglo-French fleet in 1845.

pages.title: The gaucho
pages.body: Out on the pampa lived the **gauchos**: expert horsemen, often of mixed Spanish and native roots, who worked with cattle. Knife, **boleadoras** (throwing weights borrowed from native hunters), poncho, mate and guitar. Governments treated them as vagrants and forced many into the army. Only later did they become national symbols.

pages.scenario: At a bookstore, your friend points at a book and says: 'Everyone had to read this at school. It's about a gaucho forced into the army on the frontier.'
pages.prompt: Which book is it?
pages.explain: **El gaucho Martín Fierro**, a poem by **José Hernández** (1872, with a second part in 1879). *Facundo*, by Sarmiento, is also a classic — but it's about a caudillo, not Fierro.

pages.statement: The Día de la Tradición (10 November) is celebrated on José Hernández's birthday.
pages.explain: Hernández was born on 10 November 1834. That day celebrates gaucho culture: horses, folk music, empanadas.

pages.prompt: The most quoted advice from Martín Fierro: brothers must stick together.
pages.translation: Brothers, be united.
pages.explain: 'Los hermanos sean unidos, porque esa es la ley primera.' Argentines quote it to this day.

classes.title: The frontier and the boats
classes.summary: The Campaña del Desierto, the immigration wave, conventillos, lunfardo and tango

pages.title: A country on paper
pages.body: After Rosas fell, a **Constitución** was written in **1853** (Buenos Aires joined a few years later). The new leaders had a plan: bring in European immigrants, railways and investment, and grab the land still held by the native peoples. The motto came from the thinker **Alberdi**: **gobernar es poblar**, to govern is to populate.

pages.title: The Campaña del Desierto
pages.body: Between **1878** and **1885**, the army led by **Julio Argentino Roca** took the pampa and Patagonia from the **mapuche**, **ranquel**, **tehuelche** and other peoples. Official history called it the 'desert', but it was not empty. Thousands were killed; thousands more were taken prisoner, families were split up, and many were forced to work on farms or as servants. The land went to a few big owners.

pages.title: Still debated
pages.body: For a long time schools taught it as a heroic conquest, and Roca was on the 100-peso bill. Today many historians and indigenous communities call it a **genocidio** (genocide); others reject that word and frame it as a war over territory. The debate is alive: Roca's statues get painted and argued over, and many prefer to say **Conquista del Desierto** in quotes, or not at all.

pages.statement: The 'desert' conquered in the Campaña del Desierto was an empty land.
pages.explain: It was home to mapuche, ranquel, tehuelche and other peoples. 'Desierto' was the word the state used to justify taking it.

pages.title: The boats arrive
pages.body: From the 1870s to 1930, millions of Europeans arrived, mostly **italianos** and **españoles**. In the 1914 census about **30%** of the country was foreign-born — in Buenos Aires, around half. Porteños still call any Spaniard a **gallego**, since so many came from Galicia. That's why the Italian influence is everywhere: pizza, **fainá**, **ñoquis** on the 29th, and talking with your hands.
pages.fun_fact: The old Hotel de Inmigrantes, where newcomers slept their first nights, is now a museum in Retiro.

pages.title: Life in the conventillo
pages.body: Many newcomers crammed into **conventillos**: old houses split into single rooms, one family per room, one shared patio and bathroom for dozens. Crowded, loud, mixed: Italians, Spaniards, Jews, Arabs and locals, all together. In **1907** the tenants went on a famous rent strike. La Boca's colorful **Caminito** is a tourist version of that world.

pages.title: Lunfardo and tango
pages.body: From that mix came **lunfardo**, the slang of Buenos Aires, full of Italian: **laburo** (job, from *lavoro*), **morfar** (to eat), **birra** (beer), **fiaca** (laziness). And in the outskirts of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, in the late 1800s, came **tango**, mixing habanera, **milonga** and African-rooted **candombe**. It started in humble places before it conquered Paris and the salons.

pages.scenario: Your friend groans on Monday morning: 'Uf, qué fiaca ir al laburo.'
pages.prompt: What do they mean?
options: They're too lazy to go to work
They want to eat a big lunch
They're going to a tango class
pages.explain: **Fiaca** is laziness, **laburo** is work — both from Italian, both pure lunfardo.

pages.explain: Italian roots all over: *lavoro*, *birra*, *fiacca*.

classes.title: The granary of the world
classes.summary: 1880 to 1930: trains, wheat, the secret vote and the first radio broadcast

pages.title: El granero del mundo
pages.body: Around 1900 Argentina shipped wheat, corn and beef across the ocean, mostly to Britain. British money built the railways, which fan out from the port of Buenos Aires like the ribs of a hand fan: everything flowed to the port. **Frigoríficos** (meatpacking plants) sent chilled beef to Europe. The country called itself **el granero del mundo**, the world's granary.

pages.statement: Argentina's old railway network was built mainly to connect the provinces with each other.
pages.explain: Mostly British-built, it pointed at the port of Buenos Aires, to ship grain and beef out. That's why, even today, going between two provinces can mean a long detour.

pages.title: Rich, but for whom?
pages.body: Around the **Centenario** of 1910, many Argentines felt they lived in one of the richest countries on earth, and some economic estimates agree. Buenos Aires got the Congreso and the **Teatro Colón**, which opened in 1908. But the best land was in a few hands, and many workers lived in crowded conventillos. That gap is why people still argue about how 'golden' those years were.

pages.title: Ley Sáenz Peña, 1912
pages.body: Before 1912, elections were a show: people voted out loud, the **voto cantado** (sung vote), and fraud was routine. The **Ley Sáenz Peña** made the vote **secreto** and **obligatorio** for men over 18. In 1916 **Hipólito Yrigoyen**, of the Unión Cívica Radical, won the first presidential election held that way. Women won the national vote in 1947 and cast it for the first time in 1951.

pages.scenario: It's 1905 and you walk into a polling station in Buenos Aires.
pages.prompt: How do you vote?
options: Out loud, in front of everyone
pages.explain: The **voto cantado**: you said your choice out loud, with the local boss listening. The secret ballot arrived in 1912.

pages.title: The dark side: January 1919
pages.body: In January 1919 a strike at the Vasena metal works in Buenos Aires turned into the **Semana Trágica** (Tragic Week). Under Yrigoyen's government, police, soldiers and armed civilian groups crushed it. Hundreds died (the estimates vary a lot) and thousands were arrested. Gangs also attacked the Jewish neighborhood of **Once**.

pages.title: Los locos de la azotea
pages.body: On **27 August 1920**, Enrique Susini and three friends climbed onto the roof of the Teatro Coliseo and broadcast Wagner's opera *Parsifal*. About 50 people with homemade crystal sets heard it. They were nicknamed **los locos de la azotea**, the rooftop madmen. Argentina counts it among the world's first public radio broadcasts, and 27 August is the **Día de la Radiodifusión**.

pages.prompt: What were the radio pioneers called?
pages.translation: The rooftop madmen.
pages.explain: **Azotea** is a flat roof terrace. In Buenos Aires they're everywhere, and now you know one made history.

classes.title: Coups, Perón and Evita
classes.summary: From the 1930 coup to the man who still splits family asados

pages.title: A century of coups
pages.body: Between 1930 and 1976 the army overthrew governments six times, most of them elected: in **1930, 1943, 1955, 1962, 1966 and 1976**. A coup is a **golpe de Estado**, usually just **golpe**. The 1930s got a nickname: the **Década Infame** (Infamous Decade), with elections so openly rigged that some called it *fraude patriótico*, 'patriotic fraud'.

pages.statement: Between 1930 and 1976, Argentina's military took power by force six times.
pages.explain: Six coups: 1930, 1943, 1955, 1962, 1966 and 1976. Since 1983 Argentina has had uninterrupted democracy, its longest ever.

pages.title: Enter Perón
pages.body: **Juan Domingo Perón** was an army colonel in the government born of the 1943 coup. As labour secretary he backed unions and pushed new rights for workers: pensions, paid holidays, labour courts. Many workers felt they had never had a friend that high up. The army's old guard, the bosses and much of the middle class got nervous.
pages.fun_fact: The **aguinaldo**, an extra month's pay split into June and December, was created in 1945. Argentines still count on it every year.

pages.title: 17 de octubre de 1945
pages.body: His rivals forced Perón out and locked him up on **Isla Martín García**. On **17 October 1945**, huge crowds of workers marched into Plaza de Mayo demanding his release. Some cooled their tired feet in the fountains, an image that became legend. That night Perón spoke from the balcony of the Casa Rosada. Four months later he won the presidency.

pages.scenario: It's 17 October. Your Argentine friend posts a photo of Plaza de Mayo with 'Feliz Día de la Lealtad'.
pages.prompt: What are they celebrating?
options: The 1945 workers' march that freed Perón
pages.explain: Peronists call 17 October **Día de la Lealtad**, Loyalty Day. (Maradona's birthday is close, though: 30 October.)

pages.title: Los descamisados
pages.body: Opponents sneered at Perón's supporters as **descamisados**, 'the shirtless ones': poor, rough, not fit for politics. Perón and his wife flipped the insult and wore it with pride. Workers who had felt invisible suddenly felt that the country was theirs too. That feeling of **dignidad** is the heart of what Peronists love about Perón.

pages.title: Evita
pages.body: **Eva Duarte**, a young actress from a small town in Buenos Aires province, married Perón in 1945. As **Evita** she ran a foundation that built hospitals, schools and homes, and gave aid directly to the poor. She pushed the 1947 law that gave women the vote. She died of cancer in 1952, aged 33, and millions queued for days to say goodbye.
pages.fun_fact: When Madonna came to film *Evita* in 1996, plenty of Argentines were not amused. Peronist groups protested, and graffiti against her showed up in Buenos Aires.

pages.prompt: Match the year to what happened

pages.title: Why it still splits families
pages.body: After the 1955 coup, Peronism was banned for 18 years. Perón came back, won again in 1973 and died in 1974. For supporters, Peronism means social justice and workers' rights. Critics point to censorship, a personality cult, jailed opponents and costly economics. It has had left and right wings. The political divide is called **la grieta**, 'the crack', and it often runs through the family asado.

pages.scenario: At a family asado, your girlfriend's tío grumbles that her new neighbour 'es un gorila'.
pages.prompt: What does he mean?
options: The neighbour is a great goalkeeper
pages.explain: **Gorila** is Peronist slang for an anti-Peronist. It's a jab, so keep it for when you know the room. Anti-Peronists have their own words for Peronists, too.

pages.prompt: How do Peronists name 17 October?
pages.text: El 17 de octubre es el Día de la ___.
pages.translation: 17 October is Loyalty Day.
pages.explain: **Lealtad** means loyalty: the workers' loyalty to Perón, and his to them.

classes.title: The last dictatorship
classes.summary: 1976–1983: the disappeared, the Madres and Abuelas, and 'Nunca Más'

pages.title: 24 de marzo de 1976
pages.body: After Perón died in 1974, his widow and vice-president, **Isabel Perón**, took over amid guerrilla attacks, killings by the far-right **Triple A** and economic chaos. On **24 March 1976** a military junta led by **Jorge Rafael Videla** seized power. It called itself the Proceso de Reorganización Nacional. Argentines just say **el Proceso**, or **la dictadura**.

pages.title: Los desaparecidos
pages.body: The regime hunted anyone it called 'subversive': guerrillas, but also union delegates, students, lawyers, priests, teenagers. People were kidnapped, taken to secret detention centres like the **ESMA**, tortured, and most were murdered, many thrown alive from planes into the sea or the Río de la Plata. Families got no answers. The victims became **los desaparecidos**, the disappeared.

pages.statement: In Argentina, 'los desaparecidos' refers to people who fled abroad during the dictatorship.
pages.explain: **Desaparecidos** are people the state kidnapped and made vanish, with no record, no body, no answer. Many others did go into exile, but they are called **exiliados**.

pages.title: How many?
pages.body: Human rights organisations speak of **30,000** desaparecidos, and '30.000' appears on banners every 24 March. It is an estimate: the regime destroyed its records, so a full count may never exist. The commission set up in 1984 documented close to 9,000 cases, and today's official registry lists a similar number of proven victims, disappeared or killed. The figure is contested, and when politicians question the 30,000 it sparks fierce public debate.

pages.title: Las Madres de Plaza de Mayo
pages.body: On **30 April 1977**, fourteen mothers met in Plaza de Mayo to ask where their children were. Gatherings were banned, so when police told them to move along, they walked in pairs around the pyramid. They covered their heads with **pañuelos blancos**, white headscarves, first made from their children's cloth nappies. Their founder, **Azucena Villaflor**, was herself disappeared that December.

pages.scenario: Thursday, 3:30 pm, Plaza de Mayo. A group of older women in white headscarves walk slowly around the monument in the middle.
pages.prompt: Who are they?
options: The Madres de Plaza de Mayo
pages.explain: The Madres have walked there on Thursday afternoons for decades. The white headscarf is also painted on the ground around the Pirámide de Mayo.

pages.title: Las Abuelas and the stolen babies
pages.body: Pregnant prisoners gave birth in captivity; their babies, and other children, were handed to other families, often close to the regime, under false identities. The **Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo** (grandmothers) have searched for them since 1977, helping pioneer DNA methods to prove kinship. By 2025, **140 nietos** (grandchildren) had recovered their identity, and the search goes on. Their president, **Estela de Carlotto**, found her own grandson in 2014.

pages.title: Nunca Más
pages.body: In 1984 a commission led by writer **Ernesto Sábato** published its report, **Nunca Más** ('Never Again'). In 1985, civilian judges tried the juntas in the **Juicio a las Juntas**; prosecutor **Julio Strassera** closed with 'Señores jueces: nunca más.' Videla got life. Amnesty laws and pardons followed, but they were annulled or struck down in the 2000s and trials continue today.
pages.fun_fact: The trial is the subject of the film *Argentina, 1985*, nominated for the Oscar for best international film.

pages.explain: Nearly eight years of dictatorship, then the first steps of justice.

pages.translation: Memory, Truth and Justice.
pages.explain: Every **24 de marzo** hundreds of thousands march to Plaza de Mayo, with photos of the disappeared and the chant 'Nunca más'.

classes.title: Malvinas
classes.summary: The 1982 war, the veterans, and a claim nearly every Argentine shares

pages.title: The islands
pages.body: The **Islas Malvinas** sit in the South Atlantic, about 500 km off Patagonia. Britain has held them since **1833**, when it expelled the Argentine authorities there, and Argentina has claimed them ever since. The British call them the Falklands. In Argentina, always say **Malvinas**: 'Falklands' lands very badly.

pages.scenario: At dinner in Córdoba, someone asks where you've travelled. You went to those islands in the South Atlantic.
pages.prompt: What do you call them?
pages.explain: **Las Malvinas**. Using the British name in Argentina sounds like taking sides, and it's a sore point.

pages.title: 2 de abril de 1982
pages.body: The dictatorship, now led by **Leopoldo Galtieri**, faced a collapsing economy and growing protests. On **2 April 1982** Argentine troops landed on the islands, and crowds cheered in Plaza de Mayo. Margaret Thatcher's government sent a naval task force. The war lasted 74 days. Argentina surrendered on **14 June 1982**. **649 Argentines** died, along with 255 British servicemen and 3 islanders.

pages.statement: The Malvinas war lasted about two and a half months.
pages.explain: From 2 April to 14 June 1982: 74 days.

pages.title: The soldiers
pages.body: Many who fought were **conscriptos**, 18- and 19-year-olds doing compulsory military service, known as **la colimba**. They were sent to freezing trenches, often underfed and badly equipped, and some later reported abuse from their own officers. On 2 May the cruiser **ARA General Belgrano** was sunk: 323 men died, about half of all Argentine deaths.

pages.title: Veteranos y caídos
pages.body: Today the survivors are honoured as **veteranos** or **ex combatientes**, and the dead as **los caídos**, the fallen. **2 April** is a national holiday: the Day of the Veterans and the Fallen in the Malvinas War. For years many veterans felt forgotten, and the war's wounds, physical and mental, are still an open subject.

pages.prompt: Match the date to the Malvinas memory

pages.title: Las Malvinas son argentinas
pages.body: You'll see **'Las Malvinas son argentinas'** on road signs, murals and buses. Since 1994 the claim is in the Constitution. It's one of the few things almost all Argentines agree on, across parties. The war is another matter: most see it as a doomed gamble by the dictatorship. The islanders voted in 2013 to stay British; Argentina does not accept that vote as deciding the question.

pages.scenario: Your taxi driver hears your English accent and says, half-smiling: 'Las Malvinas son argentinas, eh.'
pages.prompt: What's the best response?
options: Say 'Sí, lo sé' and ask him about it
pages.explain: It's usually a friendly-ish poke, not hostility. Listening goes a long way: many Argentines have a relative or neighbour who fought there.

pages.prompt: Complete the phrase you'll see all over the country
pages.translation: The Malvinas are Argentine.
pages.explain: **Son**, from ser: it's said as a permanent fact, and definitely not in the past tense.

pages.statement: Defeat in Malvinas helped bring down the dictatorship.
pages.explain: The defeat discredited the military. Galtieri was replaced within days, and elections were held in October 1983.

classes.title: Democracy, hyperinflation and 2001
classes.summary: From Alfonsín to 'que se vayan todos'

pages.title: Vuelve la democracia
pages.body: On 30 October 1983 **Raúl Alfonsín**, of the Radical party (UCR), won the election and took office on **10 December 1983**. He closed his rallies reciting the Preamble of the Constitution, and promised that 'con la democracia se come, se cura y se educa': with democracy, people eat, heal and learn. Every 10 December marks another year of democracy.

pages.title: Hiperinflación
pages.body: The economy didn't cooperate. Debt was huge, and a new currency, the **austral** (1985), soon crumbled. In 1989 prices went wild: yearly inflation passed **3,000%**. Supermarkets relabelled prices several times a day, and there were **saqueos**, lootings. Alfonsín handed power to the Peronist **Carlos Menem** five months early, in July 1989.

pages.scenario: It's 1989 and you just got paid in australes.
pages.prompt: What's the smart move?
options: Put it in a savings account for next year
Spend it right away, before prices go up
Frame a note as a souvenir
pages.explain: With prices climbing by the day, money lost value in your pocket. People ran to the supermarket on payday, a reflex some Argentines still have.

pages.title: Convertibilidad: 1 peso = 1 dólar
pages.body: In April 1991, Menem's economy minister **Domingo Cavallo** launched the **convertibilidad**: by law, one peso was worth one dollar, and you could swap them freely. In 1992 a new peso replaced the austral at 10,000 to one. Within a few years inflation fell to almost zero. The '90s brought privatisations, cheap imports and cheap trips abroad.
pages.fun_fact: Argentine shoppers abroad got the nickname **'deme dos'** ('give me two') in the cheap-dollar years around 1980, and it came right back in the '90s.

pages.title: The hangover
pages.body: Supporters remember the stability after years of chaos. Critics remember the rest: factories closed, unemployment passed 18% by 1995, and debt piled up to keep the peg alive. From 1998 the country was in recession, and the 1-to-1 dollar was getting hard to hold. Opinions on the '90s still split dinner tables.

pages.statement: Under convertibilidad, one peso was legally worth one US dollar.
pages.explain: From 1991 to early 2002. Many Argentines still remember when a dollar cost exactly one peso.

pages.title: Diciembre de 2001
pages.body: Under President **Fernando de la Rúa**, people rushed to pull their money out. On 1 December 2001 the government capped cash withdrawals at 250 pesos a week: the **corralito**, 'little pen'. The middle class took to the streets banging pots: the **cacerolazo**. On 19 and 20 December protests and repression left dozens dead. De la Rúa resigned and left the Casa Rosada by helicopter.

pages.title: Que se vayan todos
pages.body: The chant was **'¡Que se vayan todos!'**: 'Out with all of them', every politician. Then came five presidents in about twelve days: De la Rúa, **Ramón Puerta**, **Adolfo Rodríguez Saá** (who declared a debt default), **Eduardo Camaño** and **Eduardo Duhalde**, who took over in January 2002 and ended the 1-to-1 peso. Savings lost much of their value overnight.

classes.title: Money today: thinking in dollars
classes.summary: Inflation, the dólar blue, arbolitos and cash under the mattress

pages.title: Pesos to spend, dollars to save
pages.body: After decades of inflation, devaluations and a corralito, Argentines learned one lesson: save in dollars. Flats and cars are priced in dollars (**U$S**). Pesos are for spending, fast. Plenty of savings sit at home in cash, **bajo el colchón**, under the mattress, and Argentines are thought to hold more US banknotes per person than almost anyone outside the US.

pages.scenario: You're flat-hunting in Palermo. The listing says 'U$S 120.000'.
pages.prompt: How is a deal like this usually paid?
options: In US dollars, often in cash
pages.explain: Property is typically bought in dollars, and it's common for the notes to be counted on the spot at signing.

pages.title: Inflación, the national sport
pages.body: When the monthly inflation figure comes out, it's headline news. People **remarcan**, relabel prices, and everyone compares: '¿Viste lo que sale el café?' Yearly inflation passed 200% in 2023, then slowed sharply in 2024 and 2025. Whether it stays low is a matter of hot debate. Either way, every Argentine is a part-time economist.

pages.title: El dólar blue
pages.body: For years, buying dollars legally was capped by currency controls, the **cepo** (2011–2015, then 2019–2025). So a parallel market boomed: the **dólar blue**, usually pricier than the official rate. Nobody fully agrees why it's called 'blue'. At one point there were over a dozen dollar rates, from the **dólar tarjeta** to the short-lived **dólar Coldplay**, for paying foreign acts who played in Argentina.

pages.scenario: Walking down calle Florida in Buenos Aires, a man on the corner mutters at you: 'Cambio, cambio, dólar, euro, real...'
pages.prompt: What is he offering?
options: To swap your money on the informal market
pages.explain: He's an **arbolito**, a street money changer, offering the blue rate. They're a classic sight on Florida.

pages.title: Arbolitos y cuevas
pages.body: **Arbolito** means 'little tree': he stands on the pavement all day, like a tree. He takes you to a **cueva**, a 'cave', a back office where the swap happens. It's informal, and fake notes happen. In April 2025 people were allowed to buy dollars freely again, and the gap between blue and official shrank sharply. But the words, and the habit of checking, remain.

pages.statement: The dólar blue is a special blue banknote.
pages.explain: It's a rate, not a note. The one colour detail that matters: older US$100 bills, the **cara chica** (small face), often get a worse rate than the newer **cara grande** ones; the newest, with a blue security ribbon, are the most welcome.

pages.explain: Argentines check the dollar the way others check the weather. Ask it and you'll sound like a local.
